meta.blurb: At twenty-two, Charles Darwin took a place on a small survey ship and did not see home for almost five years. He crossed the Andes, felt an earthquake and met giant tortoises. Come along and watch him begin to wonder.
meta.bible:
Charles Darwin: English naturalist, born 12 February 1809, so 22 when the voyage began. Robert FitzRoy: the young captain of HMS Beagle, aged 26 at the start. John Henslow: Darwin's Cambridge teacher, who recommended him. The Beagle: a small British survey ship with about seventy people aboard; it left Devonport near Plymouth on 27 December 1831 and reached Falmouth on 2 October 1836. Its task was to chart coasts, especially in South America, and to measure the world's longitudes with many Chronometers. Darwin's book is the Journal of his travels, first published in 1839; later readers call it The Voyage of the Beagle. Places in order: Cape Verde Islands (the island of St Jago), Bahia and Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, Montevideo, Punta Alta, Patagonia, Port Desire, Santa Cruz, Tierra del Fuego, Woollya, the Beagle Channel, the Falkland Islands, Chiloé, Valparaíso, Valdivia, Concepción, Osorno, the Andes, Portillo, Uspallata, Lima, the Galápagos Islands, Tahiti, New Zealand, the Bay of Islands, Sydney, the Blue Mountains, the Keeling Islands, Mauritius, Cape Town, St Helena, Ascension, the Azores, Shrewsbury. People: Jemmy Button, York Minster and Fuegia Basket, three Fuegians who had been taken to England and were brought home; Richard Matthews, a missionary; Nicholas Lawson, the vice-governor of the Galápagos; Charles Lyell, author of Principles of Geology; John Gould, a bird expert; Richard Owen, an expert on fossils; John Herschel, an astronomer at Cape Town; Napoleon, whose tomb is on St Helena. Key terms: Naturalist, Specimens, Fossils, Megatherium, Glyptodon, Toxodon, Sloth, Armadillo, Gauchos, Lasso, Bolas, Rhea, Pampas, Guanacos, Warrah, Glacier, Earthquake, Volcano, Hammock, Iguanas, Tortoises, Mockingbirds, Finches, Platypus, Kangaroo, Coral, Atoll, Lagoon, Reef, Corroboree, Slavery, Fuegians, Maori, Tahitians, Aboriginal, Chronometers, Geology, Andes, Cordillera. Voice: warm, curious and plain, in the first person plural or third person; Darwin is young, keen, often seasick and always collecting. Dates and numbers are real or marked as about; nothing is invented. Added names and terms: Adam Sedgwick: Cambridge professor of geology, who took Darwin to Wales in August 1831. Josiah Wedgwood: Darwin's uncle, who persuaded Darwin's father. Robert Darwin: Darwin's father, a doctor at Shrewsbury. Shrewsbury: Darwin's home town. Cambridge: where Darwin studied. Plymouth: the port where the Beagle was fitted out. Wales: where Darwin learned geology. Clergyman: a priest, which Darwin was expected to become.
Syms Covington: a young crew member who became Darwin's helper and later his servant. Alexander von Humboldt: a German explorer whose travel book Darwin loved. Tenerife: an island in the Atlantic where the Beagle was refused landing in January 1832 for fear of Cholera; quarantine: a time of isolation. Porto Praya: the port on St Jago. St Paul's Rocks: bare rocks in the middle of the Atlantic. Fernando de Noronha: a volcanic island used by Brazil as a prison. Octopus, Seasick, Biscuits, Raisins, Pinnacle, Plankton.
Bahia: a Brazilian port, today Salvador. Rio de Janeiro: the capital of Brazil, where the Beagle arrived on 4 April 1832. Botafogo: the bay where Darwin had a cottage. Sugar Loaf: a granite mountain at the mouth of Rio bay. Rio Macaé: a river far north of Rio, which Darwin visited on horseback. Plantation, Overseer, Parliament, Hummingbirds, Orchids, Cockroaches, Convents, Chaos, Phosphorescence.
Montevideo: a town on the River Plate. Maldonado: a small town where Darwin stayed and collected. River Plate: the wide muddy estuary between Argentina and Uruguay. Bahía Blanca: a bay on the coast of Argentina. Punta Alta: a headland near Bahía Blanca, where Darwin found giant fossil bones in September 1832. Capybara: the largest rodent. Tucotuco: a small burrowing animal. Argentina, Uruguay, Estuary, Rodent, Extinct, Armoured, Brittle.
Good Success Bay: where the Beagle first met Fuegians in December 1832. Cape Horn: the southern tip of South America, with fierce storms. King William and Queen Adelaide: the royal couple who met the three Fuegians in England. Christianity, Albatrosses, Headland, Mimics, Sleet.
Falkland Islands: cold windy islands with no trees, visited in March 1833 and again in 1834; the Falkland fox, the warrah, died out in the 1870s. Río Negro: a river in Patagonia, where Darwin left the ship in August 1833. Colorado River: where General Rosas had his camp. General Rosas: Juan Manuel de Rosas, who led an army against the Indians of the plains. Buenos Aires: the capital of Argentina. Pampas: the wide grassy plains. Bolas, Mate, Poncho, Moorland, Passport, Armadillo, Boulders.
Gaucho: a horseman of the South American plains.
Santa Fe: a city on the Paraná river in Argentina. Paraná: a great river. Southern Cross: a group of stars in the southern sky. Thistles, Cardoon, Butterflies, Specimen, Diary, Catastrophe.
Patagonia: the dry southern plains of Argentina. Port Desire and Port St Julian: harbours on the Patagonian coast. Ferdinand Magellan: a Portuguese explorer who wintered at Port St Julian in 1520. Macrauchenia: a long-necked extinct animal Darwin found there. Petise: the local name for the smaller rhea. Puma, Condor, Veal, Terraces, Wilderness, Mutiny, Pebbles.
Llama: a South American animal related to the guanaco.
Strait of Magellan: the sea passage at the southern tip of South America. Mount Sarmiento: a huge snow-covered peak near the Strait. Kelp: a giant brown seaweed growing in forests under the sea. Jackass penguins: penguins that bray like donkeys. Spearheads, Fungus, Fungi, Penguins, Avalanche, Experiment.
Santa Cruz: a river and harbour in Patagonia, where the Beagle was repaired in April 1834. Port Famine: a harbour in the Strait of Magellan. Thomas Cavendish: an English sailor who named it in 1587. Mount Tarn: a mountain near Port Famine that Darwin climbed. Valparaíso: the main port of Chile, reached on 23 July 1834. Richard Corfield: Darwin's old school friend, a merchant at Valparaíso. Chile, Basalt, Whaleboats, Hull, Swells, Ruins, Merchant.
Mariano Gonzales: Darwin's Chilean guide. Madrina: the mare with a bell that leads a train of mules. Santiago: the capital of Chile. Copper, Ore, Cactus, Hospitality.

Curanto: a meal cooked in a pit with hot stones. Darwin's fox: a small dark fox of Chiloé, new to science. Osorno: a volcano in Chile that erupted on 19 January 1835. Aconcagua and Coseguina: two other volcanoes that erupted at about the same time. Nicaragua: a country in Central America. Valdivia: a small town in southern Chile. Portillo: a high pass over the Andes. Mendoza: a town of vineyards east of the Andes. Luxan: a village near Mendoza where Darwin was bitten by a benchuca. Benchuca: a blood-sucking bug of the plains. Uspallata: a mountain pass where Darwin found fossil trees on the way back. Precipice, Vineyards, Condors, Molten.
Copiapó: a desert valley in northern Chile. Iquique: a dry port with nitre works. Lima: the capital of Peru. Callao: the port of Lima. Peru: a country on the Pacific coast. San Lorenzo: an island off Callao. Galápagos Islands: volcanic islands on the equator, reached on 15 September 1835. Nitre, Saltpetre, Fertiliser, Veils.
Chatham Island, Charles Island, James Island, Albemarle: islands of the Galápagos. Marine iguanas: sea lizards that eat seaweed. Land iguanas: yellow-brown lizards that dig burrows. Hawk, Archipelago, Cactus, Pitcher, Burrows.

Blue Mountains: mountains west of Sydney. Bathurst: a town in the bush beyond them. Platypus: a duck-billed animal. Ant-lion: an insect that traps ants in a sandy pit. beats.scene: A boy fills his pockets with beetles and shells on a Shropshire hillside
beats.summary: Charles Darwin, born in 1809 at Shrewsbury, grows up collecting beetles, shells and birds' eggs instead of studying.

beats.scene: A Cambridge student holds a beetle in each hand and one in his mouth
beats.summary: At Cambridge, where he is meant to become a clergyman, Darwin hunts beetles so keenly that he puts one in his mouth when his hands are full.

beats.scene: A professor and a young student walk in a garden talking about plants
beats.summary: Professor John Henslow becomes Darwin's teacher and friend, and shows him how to look closely and write down exactly what he sees.

beats.scene: Two men tap at rocks with hammers on a Welsh hillside
beats.summary: In August 1831 Darwin goes to Wales with the geologist Adam Sedgwick and learns how to read the story told by rocks.

beats.scene: A young man reads a letter at a breakfast table with wide eyes
beats.summary: Home again, Darwin finds Henslow's letter: Captain FitzRoy wants a gentleman naturalist to sail round the world, and others have said no.

beats.scene: A stern doctor sits behind a desk, shaking his head
beats.summary: Darwin's father, Dr Robert Darwin, refuses at first, because the voyage seems a risky waste of time for a young man who should be a clergyman.

beats.scene: Two men ride in a gig through green lanes toward a country house
beats.summary: Darwin's uncle Josiah Wedgwood answers each of the father's worries, drives Darwin to Shrewsbury, and wins the father's consent.

beats.scene: In a London room, a young captain studies a visitor's face closely
beats.summary: In September 1831 FitzRoy meets Darwin; he hesitates over Darwin's nose, which he thinks shows too little energy, but the two men get on well.

beats.scene: A small ship stands in a dockyard while workmen paint and carry crates
beats.summary: At Plymouth the Beagle, a small ship about 27 metres long, is refitted, and Darwin buys microscopes, jars, guns and a geological hammer.

beats.scene: A little ship leaves a grey harbour under dark clouds while friends wave
beats.summary: Gales drive the Beagle back twice, but on 27 December 1831 she finally sails from Devonport with Darwin aboard.

beats.scene: Darwin lies pale in a hammock while waves heave beyond a porthole
beats.summary: Darwin is seasick as soon as the ship meets the swell, and he finds that lying flat and eating biscuits and raisins is the only cure.

beats.scene: A tiny cabin with a hammock above a chart table crowded with books
beats.summary: Darwin shares the small stern cabin with two young officers; he sleeps in a hammock slung above the chart table.

beats.scene: Sailors scrub the deck at dawn while Darwin watches with a notebook
beats.summary: About seventy people live and work on the Beagle, and Darwin's servant, Syms Covington, learns to skin birds and pack specimens.

beats.scene: The captain and Darwin dine together at a small table under a lamp
beats.summary: FitzRoy and Darwin dine together each evening; the captain is hot-tempered and lonely, and the two slowly become friends.

beats.scene: A small ship sits beneath a great peak with a yellow flag flying
beats.summary: At Tenerife the officials fear that the ship brings cholera and order a quarantine, so Darwin never sets foot on the island he had longed to see.

beats.scene: Darwin walks over black lava rock under a burning sun
beats.summary: At Porto Praya on the island of St Jago, Darwin takes his first walk on tropical land, among black lava, fierce sun and strange plants.

beats.scene: Darwin sits on a dark hillside with a notebook, sketching a cliff
beats.summary: In a cliff on St Jago Darwin sees a white band of seashells high above the sea, and using Lyell's ideas he decides he may write a book about the geology of the places he visits.

beats.scene: A small octopus changes colour in a rock pool while Darwin watches
beats.summary: Darwin watches an octopus change colour like a passing cloud, and drags a fine net behind the ship to catch tiny sea creatures.

beats.scene: Seabirds crowd on a bare white rock far out in the ocean
beats.summary: At St Paul's Rocks, in the middle of the Atlantic, there are no trees or soil, and the only land animals are tiny insects and spiders that live on the birds.

beats.scene: A low island with one tall rock and green trees stands in the sea
beats.summary: At Fernando de Noronha, a volcanic island used as a prison, Darwin sees the rocky peak and the forest, and Brazil is only a few days away.

beats.scene: The Beagle anchors off a green coast with white churches among palm trees
beats.summary: On 28 February 1832 the Beagle reaches Bahia in Brazil, and Darwin is eager to step ashore in the tropics at last.

beats.scene: A young man stands amazed in a dripping green forest full of butterflies
beats.summary: In the forest near Bahia, Darwin is overwhelmed by the huge leaves, the flowers and the noise; he says his mind is a chaos of delight.

beats.scene: Waves glow with green light around a ship's bow on a dark night
beats.summary: At night the sea around the Beagle glows, and Darwin looks closely at the tiny living things that make the light.

beats.scene: A broad bay circled by green mountains and a tall granite peak
beats.summary: On 4 April 1832 the Beagle enters the bay of Rio de Janeiro, with its Sugar Loaf mountain, and Darwin settles in a cottage near the shore.

beats.scene: Riders and mules climb a track through wet forest
beats.summary: Darwin joins an English party riding far north to the Rio Macaé, over a hundred miles from Rio.

beats.scene: A huge blue butterfly floats past a fig tree draped in orchids
beats.summary: On the ride Darwin collects beetles, butterflies and orchids, and lies awake listening to the frogs and insects of the forest night.

beats.scene: A column of black ants marches over a forest path
beats.summary: Darwin watches armies of small ants march through the forest, and sees spiders, cockroaches and other creatures flee from them.

beats.scene: A planter in a doorway scowls at a line of frightened people
beats.summary: On a plantation Darwin hears an angry master threaten to sell the families of his slaves apart, and he is horrified.

beats.scene: Two men face each other angrily across a ship's table
beats.summary: At dinner Darwin and FitzRoy quarrel over slavery, and the captain says they cannot live together if Darwin doubts his word.

beats.scene: The Beagle sails past a granite peak under a bright sky
beats.summary: FitzRoy apologises, the friendship holds, and in July 1832 the Beagle leaves Rio; Darwin hopes that slavery will end.

beats.scene: The ship anchors in a wide, muddy river mouth beside a low town
beats.summary: In July 1832 the Beagle reaches Montevideo on the River Plate, and Darwin begins a long stay on land while the ship surveys.

beats.scene: Darwin skins a bird at a rough table in a village house
beats.summary: At Maldonado Darwin lodges in a small house, collects birds, snakes and mammals, and learns how to prepare them for the boxes.

beats.scene: A capybara rests by a stream while Darwin approaches quietly
beats.summary: Darwin sees the capybara, the world's largest rodent, and hears the strange cry of a small burrowing animal called the tucotuco.

beats.scene: The Beagle sits at anchor off a low, muddy coast with wading birds
beats.summary: In September 1832 the Beagle reaches Bahía Blanca, and Darwin walks along the shore at Punta Alta to see what the cliffs hold.

beats.scene: A man crouches at a red cliff, picking at a huge bone
beats.summary: In the cliff at Punta Alta, Darwin finds enormous bones and teeth, though he cannot tell what animals they came from.

beats.scene: Darwin and a sailor dig out a great skull with picks
beats.summary: He digs for days and finds a huge skull and many bones, which he wraps carefully so they will not break.

beats.scene: A drawing of a giant ground sloth reaching into a tree
beats.summary: The bones belong to giant ground sloths and other huge extinct animals, relatives of the sloth and armadillo as big as elephants or rhinoceroses.

beats.scene: A small fossil tooth lies in Darwin's hand beside a horse's tooth
beats.summary: Darwin finds a horse's tooth in the same cliff, and is amazed that horses once lived in America and then vanished before the Spaniards brought new ones.

beats.scene: Darwin compares a huge armoured plate with a living armadillo on a table
beats.summary: Darwin sees that the extinct giants resemble the smaller animals still living in South America, and wonders why.

beats.scene: Crates of fossils on a ship's deck are labelled and tied
beats.summary: Darwin packs the bones with careful notes and sends them home to Henslow in Cambridge, trusting him to look after them.

beats.scene: The Beagle sails south into grey, rough seas with albatrosses overhead
beats.summary: In December 1832 the Beagle sails south from the Plate toward Tierra del Fuego, carrying three Fuegians home.

beats.scene: A ship anchors in a bay of dark hills and forest
beats.summary: On 18 December the Beagle anchors in Good Success Bay, and Darwin sees his first Fuegians shouting on a headland.

beats.scene: Fuegians with painted faces stand around a fire on a stony beach
beats.summary: The Fuegians copy the sailors' words and gestures so perfectly that Darwin is astonished at their skill as mimics.

beats.scene: A woman holds a baby in a canoe while sleet falls
beats.summary: Sleet falls on a woman and her baby who watch the ship from a canoe, and Darwin is amazed by how little the Fuegians wear in the cold.

beats.scene: A huge wave crashes across a ship's deck near a stormy cape
beats.summary: In January 1833, off Cape Horn, a huge wave strikes the Beagle and smashes a boat, and the crew fear for the ship.

beats.scene: Three people in neat English clothes stand on a ship's deck
beats.summary: Jemmy Button, York Minster and Fuegia Basket were taken to England in 1830; they learned English, and met the King and Queen, before FitzRoy took them home.

beats.scene: Jemmy Button polishes his shoes beside a ship's boat, wearing white gloves
beats.summary: Jemmy is cheerful, neat and vain about his clothes, and Darwin finds him a general favourite.

beats.scene: Wooden huts and a fenced garden stand on a bay below snowy hills
beats.summary: At Woollya FitzRoy's men build huts and plant a garden for the missionary Richard Matthews and the three Fuegians.

beats.scene: Jemmy greets his mother and brothers on a beach, awkward in his clothes
beats.summary: Jemmy meets his mother and brothers, and finds that he has half forgotten his own language, while crowds of Fuegians come to stare and take what they can.

beats.scene: The missionary Richard Matthews rows away from the shore with his belongings
beats.summary: A few days later the Beagle returns, finds Matthews robbed and frightened, and FitzRoy takes him back aboard.

beats.scene: Low brown hills, tussock grass and a few houses lie under grey mist
beats.summary: In March 1833 the Beagle reaches the windy, treeless Falkland Islands, where wild cattle and horses roam the hills.

beats.scene: A small grey fox looks fearlessly at a man on a windy green hill
beats.summary: In the Falklands Darwin meets a tame native fox, and writes that it will probably disappear once people settle the islands.

beats.scene: A river of grey boulders winds down a valley with no water
beats.summary: In the Falklands Darwin sees long streams of huge stones running down the valleys, and wonders what could have made them.

beats.scene: Darwin steps from a small boat where gauchos wait with horses
beats.summary: In August 1833 Darwin leaves the ship to ride overland with gauchos, a journey of hundreds of miles.

beats.scene: Darwin rides across a wide grassy plain with men in broad hats
beats.summary: On the pampas Darwin rides all day with the gauchos, eats beef roasted on a spear, and sleeps on the ground.

beats.scene: A great camp of tents and horses by a wide river
beats.summary: At the Colorado River Darwin visits the camp of the general Rosas, who is leading an army against the Indians, and gets a passport to use the posts.

beats.scene: Soldiers stand around a group of prisoners while Darwin looks away
beats.summary: Darwin sees how cruel the war against the Indians is, and writes of it with horror.

beats.scene: Darwin throws a rope and tangles his own horse's legs
beats.summary: Darwin tries the gauchos' throwing balls and tangles his own horse, which makes the horsemen laugh.

beats.scene: An armadillo roasts in its own shell over glowing coals
beats.summary: Roast armadillo, cooked in its shell, is meat and dish in one, and Darwin finds it very good.

beats.scene: A lone post house stands on a flat plain as a rider approaches
beats.summary: After many days in the saddle, with stops at lonely post houses, Darwin reaches Buenos Aires in September 1833.

beats.scene: Darwin crosses a wide river in a small boat with horses beside him
beats.summary: From Buenos Aires Darwin travels by river and by land to Santa Fe, and crosses the great Paraná river.

beats.scene: Red cliffs above a wide brown river show layers of shells and bones
beats.summary: In the cliffs by the Paraná Darwin finds layers of sea shells and fossil bones, proof that the sea once covered the plain.

beats.scene: Darwin rides through a field of giant thistles taller than his horse
beats.summary: Darwin sees how European thistles and cardoons have spread over huge areas of the plains, crowding out the native plants.

beats.scene: Darwin hands coins to a farmer for an enormous skull in a farmyard
beats.summary: At a farm on the Río Negro in Uruguay Darwin buys the skull of a giant animal, later called Toxodon, for eighteen pence.

beats.scene: A boy holds up a huge armoured plate patterned like stone tiles
beats.summary: Darwin finds pieces of a giant armour, which a farmer says came from an enormous armadillo, now called Glyptodon.

beats.scene: A man measures a giant jaw by candlelight with a small ruler
beats.summary: Darwin thinks about why such giants died out, and decides that rarity comes before extinction, just as illness comes before death.

beats.scene: A white cloud of butterflies swirls around a ship's rigging
beats.summary: Off the Argentine coast countless butterflies fly around the Beagle in a living snowstorm.

beats.scene: Darwin writes at a ship's table surrounded by notebooks and labelled boxes
beats.summary: Darwin keeps a diary, numbered specimen lists and long letters, and sends boxes of specimens home whenever a ship sails for England.

beats.scene: Darwin lies on his saddle cloth under a huge starry sky
beats.summary: Camping on the plains under the stars, Darwin enjoys the free life and the wide southern sky.

beats.scene: The Beagle lies in a harbour while Darwin returns with boxes of bones
beats.summary: Darwin rejoins the Beagle with his boxes, ready for the long coast of Patagonia.

beats.scene: A wide stony plain stretches empty under a pale sky
beats.summary: Patagonia is a wide, dry land of gravel and thorny bushes, yet Darwin finds that it stays in his mind for years.

beats.scene: Guanacos stand on a ridge with long necks, watching a rider
beats.summary: Guanacos, the wild cousins of the llama, watch the strangers from the ridges and cry out sharply in alarm.

beats.scene: Darwin and a sailor sit at a campfire eating a large bird
beats.summary: On Christmas Day Darwin and his friends eat a rhea, and then realise that it was the rarer second kind he wanted for study.

beats.scene: A puma roasts on a spit while sailors eat and look doubtful
beats.summary: Darwin eats puma meat, which he finds white and tasting like veal, and sees how pumas hunt the guanacos.

beats.scene: A weathered gallows post stands on a bare headland by a harbour
beats.summary: At Port St Julian, where Magellan once faced a mutiny, the Beagle stops for several days.

beats.scene: Darwin kneels in clay lifting a long neck bone
beats.summary: At Port St Julian Darwin finds the bones of a long-necked giant, later called Macrauchenia, which looks like an enormous llama.

beats.scene: Pebble plains rise in great steps toward distant hills
beats.summary: Darwin sees that the plains of Patagonia are a series of great stairs made of shingle, which were once beaches.

beats.scene: A condor circles on wide wings above sea cliffs
beats.summary: A condor soars above the cliffs on wings about three metres wide, hardly beating them once.

beats.scene: Guanaco bones lie piled beside a river under bright sun
beats.summary: Darwin notices that guanacos seem to go to the same places by the rivers to die, and the ground there is white with bones.

beats.scene: Two kinds of rhea stand on either side of a river on a map
beats.summary: Darwin learns that the two kinds of rhea live in different parts of the land, one replacing the other, and wonders why.

beats.scene: The Beagle sails into a narrow channel between steep forested slopes and snow
beats.summary: In early 1834 the Beagle enters the Beagle Channel again, a long strait of forests below snowy mountains.

beats.scene: Giant kelp floats in dark water around a rowing boat
beats.summary: Darwin sees forests of giant kelp, growing in the sea, which shelter thousands of animals, and says that they rival tropical forests.

beats.scene: A blue glacier meets the sea as small boats row from a falling wave
beats.summary: Darwin sees glaciers reaching the sea, and a falling piece of ice makes a huge wave that nearly wrecks the boats.

beats.scene: Fuegian canoes with small fires burning in them come near the Beagle
beats.summary: Darwin watches the Fuegians who live on shellfish in canoes with fires, and is struck by how they survive such cold.

beats.scene: A thin man in a ragged blanket greets a boat from the Beagle
beats.summary: A year later the Beagle reaches Woollya and finds Jemmy Button thin and dressed in a blanket, but glad to see them.

beats.scene: Jemmy Button sits at a table, holding a knife and fork neatly
beats.summary: Jemmy dines with FitzRoy as politely as ever, and says that he is happy and does not want to go to England again.

beats.scene: A small fire burns on the shore at sunset as a ship sails away
beats.summary: When the Beagle leaves, Jemmy lights a farewell fire on the shore, and Darwin hears how York Minster had robbed him and left.

beats.scene: Yellow round fungi grow on a beech tree in a rainy forest
beats.summary: Darwin notes the round yellow fungus growing on the beech trees, which the Fuegians use as an important food.

beats.scene: A dark peak of snow and ice rises above a grey sea
beats.summary: Darwin sees Mount Sarmiento, a huge cone of ice and snow rising straight from the sea, and thinks it the grandest sight of the voyage.

beats.scene: Penguins stand on a grassy shore beside a calm bay
beats.summary: Back in the Falklands, Darwin watches the jackass penguins that stand like men on the shore, bray like donkeys and swim like fish.

beats.scene: The Beagle leans on a beach at low tide while sailors scrape her hull
beats.summary: At Santa Cruz the crew beaches the Beagle at low tide to repair and clean her.

beats.scene: Three whaleboats row up a wide grey river beneath stony cliffs
beats.summary: FitzRoy, Darwin and about twenty-five men set off in three whaleboats to explore the Santa Cruz River, taking food for three weeks.

beats.scene: Men walk along the bank hauling boats with long ropes
beats.summary: The current is strong, so the men walk along the bank and haul the boats upstream with ropes, and Darwin helps.

beats.scene: Dark cliffs of basalt line a valley with milky blue water
beats.summary: Darwin sees black layers of basalt in the cliffs, and boulders carried down from the Andes by the milky blue river.

beats.scene: A line of distant blue peaks rises above a dry plain at evening
beats.summary: After about two weeks the party sees the snowy Andes in the distance, but the food is half gone, and FitzRoy decides to turn back.

beats.scene: Three boats race downstream under a blue sky
beats.summary: The boats are carried down the river in a fraction of the time, and the party is back on the Beagle within days.

beats.scene: The Beagle rounds into the Strait of Magellan under dark mountains
beats.summary: The Beagle sails into the Strait of Magellan and reaches Port Famine, named by an English sailor after the Spanish colonists who starved there.

beats.scene: Darwin climbs a snowy slope through beech trees to a summit
beats.summary: Darwin climbs Mount Tarn, about 800 metres high, and sees a huge view of snowy mountains and channels.

beats.scene: A ship passes between cliffs into a wide, rolling ocean
beats.summary: In June 1834 the Beagle leaves the Strait and enters the Pacific Ocean, and Darwin looks forward to a warmer climate.

beats.scene: The Beagle sails into Valparaiso harbour with white houses on steep hills
beats.summary: On 23 July 1834 the Beagle reaches Valparaíso, in Chile, where Darwin meets his old school friend Richard Corfield.

beats.scene: Brown dry hills with cactus rise above a harbour in bright sunshine
beats.summary: After the grey south, Chile's dry brown hills, cactus and warm sun delight Darwin.

beats.scene: Darwin and Mariano Gonzales load mules at dawn
beats.summary: In August 1834 Darwin hires a guide, Mariano Gonzales, and ten mules following a mare with a bell, and sets off to explore the country.

beats.scene: A long mule train climbs a zigzag path in a steep valley
beats.summary: Darwin rides over the dry hills and through green valleys to Santiago and then to the mines of the south.

beats.scene: A miner climbs a notched log ladder carrying a heavy sack of ore
beats.summary: In a copper mine Darwin sees the miners carry enormous loads of ore up steep ladders, and is amazed at their strength.

beats.scene: A farm family in a yard offers bread and fruit to Darwin
beats.summary: In Chile no one will take payment for a night's lodging, and Darwin is fed and welcomed at every farm.

beats.scene: Snow peaks glow pink above a green valley with poplar trees
beats.summary: From Santiago Darwin sees the Andes glow in the evening light, and begins to plan a journey across them.

beats.scene: Darwin picks sea shells from a layer of rock on a high hill
beats.summary: On the hills Darwin finds sea shells far above the shore, and sees that Chile's coast has risen.

beats.scene: Darwin lies feverish in bed, a sunlit window beside him
beats.summary: In late September 1834 Darwin falls ill with a fever, probably from bad food or water, and goes to bed.

beats.scene: Darwin in bed reads a book while sunlight crosses the sheets
beats.summary: Corfield cares for him in his own house, and Darwin spends about a month in bed, thinking and writing.

beats.scene: The Beagle leaves Valparaiso on a clear morning with the Andes beyond
beats.summary: On 10 November 1834 the Beagle leaves Valparaíso, and Darwin, thinner but stronger, goes with her.

beats.scene: Tall dark trees come down to a quiet grey sea in rain
beats.summary: The Beagle reaches the island of Chiloé in Chile, a rainy land of thick forest and small villages.

beats.scene: A small dark fox watches surveyors on a rocky shore
beats.summary: At Chiloé a small fox is so absorbed in watching the surveyors that Darwin can walk right up to it, and it proves to be a new species.

beats.scene: Darwin wades through a tangle of bamboo and giant ferns in a wet forest
beats.summary: The forests of Chiloé are so thick that Darwin has to climb along fallen trunks, and cannot see more than a few steps ahead.

beats.scene: A quiet town of wooden houses with grass growing in its streets
beats.summary: Darwin rides to Castro, the old capital of Chiloé, a quiet town of wooden houses where grass grows in the streets.

beats.scene: A family cooks shellfish and potatoes in a pit with hot stones
beats.summary: The people of Chiloé are poor but kind; they cook their food in a hole in the ground, between hot stones.

beats.scene: Darwin digs up a small wild potato plant on a wet shore
beats.summary: In the Chonos Islands Darwin finds wild potatoes growing on the beaches, and learns that the potato comes from this part of the world.

beats.scene: A snow-capped volcano smokes against a night sky, seen across dark water
beats.summary: From Chiloé Darwin sees the volcano Osorno burst into eruption on 19 January 1835, lighting the night.

beats.scene: Three volcano symbols are linked by a dotted line across a map
beats.summary: Darwin later learns that two other volcanoes erupted at about the same time, one far to the north in Nicaragua.

beats.scene: The Beagle enters a river bay with green hills and orchards at Valdivia
beats.summary: In February 1835 the Beagle reaches Valdivia, a small town in the forest of Chile, famed for its apples.

beats.scene: Darwin strolls through an orchard laden with apples beside a smiling boy
beats.summary: Darwin enjoys the apple orchards and the cider of Valdivia, not knowing that the next day he will feel the earth move.

beats.scene: Darwin rests under a tree in a forest while the ground ripples
beats.summary: On 20 February 1835, while Darwin is resting on the ground at Valdivia, a powerful earthquake shakes the land.

beats.scene: Trees sway and the ground trembles while Darwin tries to stand
beats.summary: The earthquake lasts about two minutes, and Darwin says it was like walking on thin ice that bends beneath his feet.

beats.scene: A man sits on the road, looking at his hands as the earth settles
beats.summary: Darwin writes that an earthquake destroys the oldest ideas in a moment, for the very symbol of solidity has moved beneath us.

beats.scene: White waves cross a bay and small boats lie flung on the shore
beats.summary: At Valdivia the damage is small, but the sea behaves strangely, and word comes that Concepción has suffered terribly.

beats.scene: The Beagle enters a bay beside a ruined town of tumbled walls
beats.summary: On 4 March 1835 the Beagle reaches Concepción and Talcahuano and finds the towns in ruins.

beats.scene: People camp in huts of branches beside cracked walls while children play
beats.summary: Most of the people of Concepción survived, because the shock was slow enough to let them run into the streets; at night the loss would have been far worse.

beats.scene: A great wave rolls over a shore, carrying timber and boats
beats.summary: A huge sea wave swept over the shore after the earthquake, carrying boats and timber far inland.

beats.scene: Sailors measure a line of mussel shells lying above the water on rocks
beats.summary: Darwin and FitzRoy find that the land near Concepción has risen by two or three feet, and mussel beds that once lay under water are high and dry.

beats.scene: A rocky island has a white strip of dead shellfish high above the sea
beats.summary: At Santa Maria island the land has risen about three metres, and Darwin walks over old mussel beds far above the tide.

beats.scene: Darwin and FitzRoy discuss a chart showing the Pacific coast
beats.summary: Darwin concludes that earthquakes and volcanoes come from the same cause, and that raising land by small jerks is how mountain ranges grow.

beats.scene: Darwin and Mariano Gonzales set out with mules at sunrise
beats.summary: In March 1835 Darwin returns to Santiago and sets out again with Mariano Gonzales and a train of mules, to cross the Andes.

beats.scene: A long line of mules winds up a narrow valley beside a roaring river
beats.summary: They follow a deep valley with steep cliffs on both sides, where the path narrows and the mules tread carefully.

beats.scene: Mules with bells cross deep snow beneath a blue sky
beats.summary: At the top the snow lies deep, and the line of mules and men slowly crosses the high pass of Portillo.

beats.scene: A layer of seashells in grey rock sits near a snowy summit
beats.summary: High in the Andes, Darwin finds fossil seashells in the rock, more than 3,500 metres above the sea.

beats.scene: Darwin stands on a ridge looking east over a plain like a sea
beats.summary: From the highest pass Darwin looks east over a plain as flat and wide as the sea, and sees how different the two sides of the mountains are.

beats.scene: Darwin sits breathless on a rock while the mules rest
beats.summary: In the thin air Darwin gasps for breath, and his guide blames the snow, but Darwin thinks the real cause is the height.

beats.scene: Darwin rides into a town of vineyards and orchards below the mountains
beats.summary: Darwin reaches Mendoza, a town of vineyards, fig trees and peaches on the dry plain east of the Andes.

beats.scene: A dark insect climbs a wall of a hut at night while Darwin watches
beats.summary: At Luxan a blood-sucking bug called the benchuca bites Darwin; some scientists think it may have given him a lasting illness, though this is still debated.

beats.scene: A row of stone trees stands upright on a bare mountain slope
beats.summary: At Uspallata, on the way back, Darwin finds a group of fossil trees standing upright, which grew near the sea and have since been lifted high.

beats.scene: Darwin sits on a rock looking at the Andes at sunset with a notebook
beats.summary: Darwin concludes that the Andes were raised bit by bit over a very long time, just as Lyell had taught.

beats.scene: The Beagle sails north along a barren, dry coast with pale cliffs
beats.summary: Darwin returns to the ship, which sails north along a brown, dry coast where little grows.

beats.scene: A dry stony valley with grey shrubs and a thin line of green farms
beats.summary: In June 1835 Darwin rides to Copiapó through desert valleys where rain may not fall for years, and farms grow only beside the rivers.

beats.scene: A dry port town beneath bare cliffs with water barrels on a quay
beats.summary: At Iquique there is no fresh water, and the people bring it by boat; Darwin visits the nitre works nearby, where the earth is dug for saltpetre.

beats.scene: A grey, misty city with flat roofs seen from the sea
beats.summary: In July 1835 the Beagle reaches Callao and Lima, in Peru, a city under a grey sky where it hardly ever rains.

beats.scene: Women in black veils with one eye uncovered walk along a Lima street
beats.summary: Darwin sees the women of Lima in black veils that leave only one eye uncovered, and finds the city dusty and dull.

beats.scene: Broken walls of an old town stand by a grey sea
beats.summary: Darwin sees the ruins of old Callao, which was destroyed in 1746 by an earthquake and a great sea wave.

beats.scene: A layer of shells lies high on a rocky island above the water
beats.summary: On San Lorenzo island Darwin finds sea shells, and even bits of string and corn, about twenty-five metres above the sea, a sign that this coast has risen within human history.

beats.scene: Chronometers lie in rows in padded boxes while FitzRoy checks them
beats.summary: FitzRoy's great task is to measure longitude around the world, and he checks his more than twenty clocks against the stars.

beats.scene: The Beagle sails west across an empty ocean at sunset
beats.summary: On 7 September 1835 the Beagle leaves Peru and sails west across the Pacific toward the Galápagos Islands.

beats.scene: Low black hills and a cinder cone appear on the horizon
beats.summary: On 15 September 1835 the crew sights the Galápagos Islands, a group of black volcanic islands on the equator.

beats.scene: Sailors row ashore at a lava beach where surf crashes on black rock
beats.summary: On Chatham Island, Darwin finds hot black lava, leafless bushes and a silence that feels unearthly.

beats.scene: A dark lizard with a spiny back swims in the sea beside black rocks
beats.summary: Darwin watches the marine iguanas, which swim in the sea and eat seaweed, and calls them imps of darkness.

beats.scene: Darwin sits by a tent surrounded by burrows and yellow land iguanas
beats.summary: On James Island Darwin camps for several days among land iguanas, which are so many that he can hardly find a spot for his tent.

beats.scene: Giant tortoises plod along a worn track to a spring in the highlands
beats.summary: Darwin watches giant tortoises on their long walk to the springs, and learns that early sailors found water by following their paths.

beats.scene: Darwin sits astride a huge tortoise in a dry highland
beats.summary: Darwin rides a giant tortoise, and the vice-governor Lawson tells him he can tell which island a tortoise comes from by its shell.

beats.scene: Sailors cook tortoise meat over a fire beside a stack of live tortoises
beats.summary: Sailors take live tortoises aboard for fresh meat, and Darwin eats it too, but learns that so many have been taken that some islands have few left.

beats.scene: Two mockingbirds on separate dry branches, each slightly different
beats.summary: Darwin notices that the mockingbirds on different islands look slightly different, and wonders whether each island has its own kind.

beats.scene: A tray of small brown finches with beaks of different shapes
beats.summary: Darwin collects small finches but does not label which island each one came from, and only later learns that they are many kinds.

beats.scene: A small hawk sits still on a branch while a gun barrel touches it
beats.summary: The birds and animals of the Galápagos are so tame that Darwin pushes a hawk off a branch with the end of his gun.

beats.scene: A map of black islands arranged in a wide circle in the sea
beats.summary: Darwin sees that each island has its own kinds, all related to those of South America, and calls the islands a little world within themselves.

beats.scene: The Beagle sails west under full canvas with flying fish leaping
beats.summary: In late October 1835 the Beagle leaves the Galápagos and sails more than three weeks across the open Pacific.

beats.scene: A low ring island with palm trees and white surf lies around a lagoon
beats.summary: In the Low Archipelago Darwin sees his first ring of coral land around a lagoon, a thin line of white surf and palms.

beats.scene: High green peaks rise above surf, canoes and a white beach
beats.summary: In November 1835 the Beagle reaches Tahiti, where Darwin climbs a valley and admires the friendly, cheerful people.

beats.scene: Tahitians offer coconuts and bananas to Darwin while children laugh
beats.summary: The Tahitians greet the visitors with fruit and laughter, wearing white cloth and flowers, and Darwin finds them gentle and handsome.

beats.scene: Darwin and two guides cross a stream in a deep green valley
beats.summary: Darwin sets out inland with two guides, who carry food and water in bamboo tubes and catch fish with their hands.

beats.scene: A waterfall plunges down a steep green wall beneath tree ferns
beats.summary: The party climbs a cliff by ropes of vine, and from the top the valley opens below, full of waterfalls, ferns and fruit trees.

beats.scene: A simple white church with a crowd of Tahitians in white clothes
beats.summary: On Sunday Darwin attends a Tahitian church, and is struck by how orderly and attentive the congregation is.

beats.scene: Darwin sits with village chiefs in a hut, writing notes
beats.summary: Darwin believes the missionaries have done much good in Tahiti, and answers critics who say the islanders were better off before.

beats.scene: A view from a high peak over a reef around a neighbouring island
beats.summary: From a mountain Darwin sees the island of Eimeo ringed by a reef and lagoon, which fits his growing idea of how coral rings form.

beats.scene: The Beagle leaves Tahiti while the island fades into purple clouds
beats.summary: On 26 November 1835 the Beagle leaves Tahiti, bound for New Zealand, and Darwin is seasick again.

beats.scene: A flat grassy bay with a wooden farmhouse and a small English-looking church
beats.summary: In December 1835 the Beagle reaches the Bay of Islands in New Zealand, where Darwin visits an English mission among Maori villages.

beats.scene: A Maori man with a tattooed face stands in a feather cloak beside canoes
beats.summary: Darwin meets the Maori, a proud and energetic people with carved tattoos, and notes how different they are from the Fuegians.

beats.scene: Darwin walks with a missionary through ferns toward a farm with sheep
beats.summary: Darwin walks to Waimate, an English-style farm with hedges, hops and wheat, set in the middle of the New Zealand bush.

beats.scene: A rough port street with drunken sailors and half-built wooden houses
beats.summary: At Kororareka Darwin sees a rough town of runaway sailors and drinkers, and is shocked.

beats.scene: The Beagle leaves New Zealand while a Maori canoe waves from the shore
beats.summary: On 30 December 1835 the Beagle leaves New Zealand, and Darwin writes that they are all glad to leave.

beats.scene: A bright new harbour town with sails and stone houses beneath wooded hills
beats.summary: In January 1836 the Beagle reaches Sydney, and Darwin is astonished to see how fast the young city has grown.

beats.scene: Darwin rides with a guide through blue-tinted gum trees across the Blue Mountains
beats.summary: Darwin rides inland across the Blue Mountains and notices how the leaves of the gum trees hang edgeways and give little shade.

beats.scene: A small duck-billed animal swims in a quiet pond near a bush track
beats.summary: At Bathurst Darwin watches a platypus, and an ant-lion's pit like those of Europe, and reflects on one Creator and many kinds.

beats.scene: Aboriginal men dance by firelight in a clearing while Darwin watches from a log
beats.summary: Darwin watches a gathering of Aboriginal people dancing at night, and writes that settlers' arrival has brought great harm to them.

beats.scene: A mountain with a mist-covered summit rises above a small harbour
beats.summary: In February 1836 the Beagle reaches Hobart in Van Diemen's Land, where Darwin learns that the island's Aboriginal people have been moved away by the settlers.

beats.scene: A low ring of white sand and palm trees surrounds a calm turquoise lagoon
beats.summary: In April 1836 the Beagle reaches the Keeling Islands, a ring of coral and palms around a quiet lagoon.

beats.scene: Darwin stands on a reef edge as huge waves break on the outer side
beats.summary: On the outer reef huge waves break all day, yet living coral and pink algae hold the wall firm, and Darwin admires them.

beats.scene: A giant crab opens a coconut under a palm with its great claws
beats.summary: Darwin learns about the robber crab, a giant land crab that climbs palm trees and opens coconuts with its claws.

beats.scene: A sinking island with a growing coral ring around it, drawn in three stages
beats.summary: Darwin explains how coral rings form: an island slowly sinks while the coral on its edge grows upward, leaving a ring around a lagoon.

beats.scene: The Beagle anchors off a green island with sharp peaks and sugar fields
beats.summary: At Mauritius, in the Indian Ocean, the Beagle's crew are warmly welcomed, and Darwin sees sugar fields and rough mountains.

beats.scene: Darwin shakes hands with a tall astronomer in a garden below a flat mountain
beats.summary: At Cape Town Darwin has the honour of meeting the famous astronomer Sir John Herschel.

beats.scene: A small solitary grave stands under a willow on a steep green island
beats.summary: On St Helena, Darwin visits Napoleon's grave, and sees how goats have destroyed the island's original forest.

beats.scene: Darwin reads a letter by lamplight with a happy face
beats.summary: At Ascension, Darwin finds letters saying that Henslow has read his notes to scientists, and that his collections are already admired at home.

beats.scene: Darwin leans on the ship's rail looking at an empty horizon
beats.summary: To check the chronometers FitzRoy sails back to Bahia, and Darwin, longing for home, is furious at the delay and glad to leave Brazil forever.

beats.scene: A green island rises from a grey sea beneath low cloud
beats.summary: The Beagle sails to the Azores and then north through autumn storms, and Darwin feels his home drawing near.

beats.scene: A small ship comes into a green harbour on an autumn morning
beats.summary: On 2 October 1836 the Beagle reaches Falmouth in England, after four years and nine months, and Darwin hurries home.

beats.scene: Darwin rides in a night coach through dark English lanes
beats.summary: Darwin takes the coach north, and reaches Shrewsbury in the night, and sleeps in his own bed.

beats.scene: A family at a breakfast table looks up in surprise as Darwin enters
beats.summary: In the morning his family, astonished to see him, sit down to breakfast; his father says that the shape of his head has altered.

beats.scene: Darwin hands boxes of fossils and birds to experts in a museum workshop
beats.summary: Darwin gives his fossils and birds to experts such as Richard Owen and John Gould, who identify them.

beats.scene: A bird expert points to a tray of finches and explains to Darwin
beats.summary: In 1837 Gould tells Darwin that the finches of the Galápagos are a group of many related kinds, and that the mockingbirds differ from island to island.

beats.scene: A notebook open to a sketch of a branching tree
beats.summary: In 1837 Darwin begins secret notebooks on how species change, and sketches a tree of life.

beats.scene: Darwin reads a book by lamplight with a puzzled, excited look
beats.summary: In 1838 Darwin reads a famous essay on population by Thomas Malthus, and sees how the struggle for life could change species over time.

beats.scene: A bound book with a ship on its cover lies on a desk
beats.summary: In 1839 Darwin publishes his Journal of the voyage, which becomes a popular book, later called The Voyage of the Beagle.

beats.scene: A weathered ship at a quay at dusk with a coastguard flag
beats.summary: The Beagle makes one more survey voyage, then ends as a coastguard watch ship and is sold and broken up in 1870.

beats.scene: An old man writes at a desk beside a window with a weather map
beats.summary: Darwin later called the voyage the most important event of his life; FitzRoy later helped found weather forecasting.

A1A2: Charles Darwin was a boy who loved collecting beetles, shells and eggs.
At Cambridge, Darwin put a beetle in his mouth because his hands were full.
Professor Henslow taught Darwin to look closely and to write down everything.
In 1831, Darwin went to Wales with Sedgwick to learn about rocks.
A letter from Henslow said that a captain needed a young naturalist.
His father said no because he thought the trip was a waste of time.
Darwin's uncle, Josiah Wedgwood, answered every worry, and the father said yes.
In London, Captain FitzRoy looked at Darwin's nose and almost said no.
The Beagle was a small ship, and workers made her ready at Plymouth.
After two false starts, the Beagle finally sailed on 27 December 1831.
Darwin felt very sick on the ship and lay in his hammock.
Darwin shared a tiny cabin and slept above the chart table.
About seventy people worked on the Beagle, and Syms Covington helped Darwin.
Every evening, Darwin ate dinner with the captain, and they became friends.
At Tenerife, officials feared sickness on the ship, so nobody could land.
On St Jago, Darwin walked on black rocks in the hot sun.
Darwin read Lyell's book and began to think about writing his own.
Darwin watched an octopus change colour and caught tiny sea animals in a net.
St Paul's Rocks is a tiny place with only birds and insects.
At Fernando de Noronha, Darwin saw a rocky island with green trees.
On 28 February 1832, the Beagle arrived at Bahia, in Brazil.
In the forest, Darwin saw huge trees and flowers, and he felt amazed.
At night, the sea around the ship shone with a green light.
In April, the Beagle entered the beautiful bay of Rio de Janeiro.
Darwin joined some Englishmen and rode on horseback far into the countryside.
Darwin collected butterflies and beetles, and he heard frogs singing at night.
Darwin watched long lines of ants, and other small animals ran away.
On a farm, Darwin heard a man threaten to sell slave families apart.
At dinner, Darwin and FitzRoy argued about slavery, and the captain became angry.
FitzRoy said sorry, and the Beagle left Rio in July 1832.
In July 1832, the Beagle reached Montevideo, near a wide muddy river.
At Maldonado, Darwin stayed in a small house and collected birds and snakes.
Darwin saw a huge animal called a capybara beside a river.
In September 1832, Darwin walked along the shore near Bahía Blanca.
In a low cliff, Darwin found huge bones and teeth.
Darwin and a sailor dug out a huge skull and wrapped it carefully.
The bones belonged to giant animals that no longer live anywhere.
Darwin found a horse's tooth in the cliff, and he was very surprised.
Darwin saw that the old giants looked like small animals alive today.
Darwin packed the bones carefully and sent them to Henslow in England.
In December 1832, the Beagle sailed south toward the cold end of America.
On 18 December, Darwin saw Fuegians for the first time, shouting on a hill.
The Fuegians copied the sailors' words and movements very well.
Sleet fell on a woman and her baby, but they wore almost nothing.
Near Cape Horn, a huge wave hit the ship and broke a boat.
Jemmy, York and Fuegia had lived in England and learned English.
Jemmy kept his shoes shiny, and everyone on the ship liked him.
At Woollya, the sailors built huts and made a garden for the missionary.
Jemmy met his mother and brothers, but he had forgotten much of his language.
Matthews was robbed and afraid, so FitzRoy took him back to the ship.
In March 1833, the Beagle reached the windy Falkland Islands, which have no trees.
A small fox in the Falklands came close to Darwin without fear.
Darwin saw rivers of huge stones running down the valleys.
In August 1833, Darwin left the ship to ride across the land.
Darwin rode all day with gauchos and slept on the ground at night.
Darwin visited the camp of General Rosas, who led an army.
Darwin saw how cruel the war against the Indians was, and he was shocked.
Darwin tried to throw a rope like a gaucho, but he caught his own horse.
Darwin ate an armadillo cooked in its own shell, and he liked it.
After many days on horseback, Darwin reached the city of Buenos Aires.
Darwin travelled north by boat and horse to the town of Santa Fe.
In the river cliffs, Darwin found sea shells and old bones.
Darwin rode through fields of huge thistles that were taller than his horse.
At a farm in Uruguay, Darwin bought a huge skull very cheaply.
Darwin also found pieces of giant armour from an enormous animal.
Darwin thought about why such big animals had died out.
Thousands of white butterflies flew around the Beagle like snow.
Darwin wrote in his diary every day and sent boxes home.
Darwin slept on the plains and looked up at the stars.
In November 1833, Darwin returned to the Beagle with boxes of bones.
Patagonia is a wide, dry land with many stones and few plants.
Guanacos are wild animals like llamas, and they watched Darwin from the hills.
At Christmas, Darwin ate a rare bird before he knew what it was.
Darwin ate puma meat, and he said it was white and tasted good.
Magellan, a famous sailor, once stayed at Port St Julian for the winter.
Darwin found the bones of a huge animal like an enormous llama.
The plains of Patagonia rise in great steps, like stairs for giants.
A condor flew over the cliffs and hardly moved its wings.
Darwin saw many bones where guanacos go to die by the river.
Darwin learned that two kinds of rhea live in different places.
In 1834, the Beagle sailed again into the long, narrow Beagle Channel.
Darwin saw giant seaweed growing like forests in the cold sea.
At a glacier, falling ice made a huge wave and nearly broke the boats.
Darwin watched Fuegians in canoes who lived near the shore and ate fish.
A year later, Jemmy Button looked thin and wore only a blanket.
Jemmy ate dinner politely with FitzRoy and said he was happy.
As the ship left, Jemmy lit a fire on the shore.
Darwin found round yellow fungi on the trees that the Fuegians eat.
Darwin saw Mount Sarmiento, a huge mountain of ice and snow.
In the Falklands, Darwin watched penguins that stood upright like little men.
At Santa Cruz, the crew pulled the Beagle onto a beach for repairs.
FitzRoy, Darwin and many men set out in three small boats.
The river was strong, so the men pulled the boats with ropes.
Darwin saw black cliffs beside a river with milky blue water.
They saw the Andes far away, but their food was nearly half gone.
On the way home, the river carried the boats quickly downstream.
The Beagle sailed into the Strait of Magellan and reached Port Famine.
Darwin climbed Mount Tarn and saw snowy mountains in every direction.
In June 1834, the Beagle left the Strait and entered the Pacific Ocean.
At Valparaíso, in Chile, Darwin met his old school friend Richard Corfield.
After the cold south, Darwin enjoyed the warm sun of Chile.
In August, Darwin hired a guide named Mariano Gonzales and ten mules.
Darwin rode over dry hills and green valleys to the city of Santiago.
In a copper mine, Darwin saw men carry very heavy loads.
At every farm, people gave Darwin food and a bed for free.
From Santiago, Darwin saw the Andes shine pink in the evening light.
On the hills, Darwin found sea shells far above the sea.
In September, Darwin became ill with a fever and lay in bed.
Corfield looked after Darwin in his house for about a month.
On 10 November 1834, the Beagle left Valparaíso, and Darwin went with her.
The Beagle reached Chiloé, an island with rain and thick green forest.
A small fox watched the sailors so closely that Darwin walked up to it.
The forest was so thick that Darwin had to climb over fallen trees.
Darwin rode to Castro, a quiet old town with grass in the streets.
The people of Chiloé cooked their food in a hole with hot stones.
In the islands nearby, Darwin found wild potatoes growing on the beach.
On the night of 19 January 1835, Darwin saw the volcano Osorno burst into fire.
Darwin later learned that two other volcanoes erupted at about the same time.
In February 1835, the Beagle reached Valdivia, a small town in the forest.
Darwin walked among apple trees and enjoyed the cider of Valdivia.
On 20 February 1835, Darwin was resting in a forest near Valdivia.
Suddenly, the ground began to shake, and Darwin could hardly stand.
Darwin thought that the solid earth was not safe at all.
At Valdivia the damage was small, but other towns suffered badly.
On 4 March, the Beagle reached Concepción and found the town in ruins.
Most people had survived, and they lived in small huts made of branches.
A huge wave from the sea washed boats and wood far inland.
Darwin and FitzRoy saw that the land had risen by two or three feet.
On Santa Maria island, the land had risen about three metres.
Darwin decided that earthquakes and volcanoes come from the same cause.
In March 1835, Darwin set out with his guide to cross the Andes.
They followed a deep valley with steep cliffs and a noisy river.
At the top of the pass, the snow was deep.
High in the mountains, Darwin found fossil sea shells in the rock.
From the top, Darwin saw a huge plain that looked like the sea.
In the thin air, Darwin found it hard to breathe.
In Mendoza, Darwin saw fields of grapes, figs and peaches.
At night a blood-sucking bug bit Darwin, and it may have made him ill.
On the way back, Darwin found trees that had turned to stone.
Darwin decided that the Andes grew slowly over a very long time.
After his trip, Darwin joined the ship, which sailed north along a dry coast.
In the north, Darwin rode through a desert where rain hardly ever falls.
At Iquique, there was no fresh water, so ships had to bring it.
In July 1835, the Beagle reached Lima, in Peru, under a grey sky.
Women in Lima wore black veils, and only one eye showed.
Darwin saw the ruins of old Callao, which a huge wave destroyed.
On San Lorenzo island, Darwin found sea shells high above the sea.
FitzRoy used more than twenty clocks to measure places on the Earth.
On 7 September 1835, the Beagle left Peru and sailed west.
On 15 September, the crew saw the black islands called the Galápagos.
On Chatham Island, the ground was black rock, and the sun was hot.
Darwin saw sea lizards that swam in the sea and ate seaweed.
On James Island, Darwin put up a tent among many land lizards.
Giant tortoises walk very slowly along old paths to a spring.
Darwin rode a giant tortoise, and Lawson said every island has its own kind.
Sailors took live tortoises on the ship to eat fresh meat.
Darwin saw that the birds on different islands looked a little different.
Darwin collected small finches but did not write down where he found them.
The birds were so tame that Darwin pushed a hawk with his gun.
Darwin said the Galápagos Islands were a little world of their own.
In October 1835, the Beagle left the Galápagos and crossed the Pacific.
Darwin saw his first coral island, a ring of palms around a lagoon.
On 15 November 1835, the Beagle came to the green island of Tahiti.
The Tahitians gave Darwin fruit and smiled, and he thought they were gentle.
Darwin walked inland with two guides, who caught fish with their hands.
They climbed a cliff with ropes and saw waterfalls and tall trees.
On Sunday, Darwin went to a Tahitian church and saw quiet, polite people.
Darwin said that the missionaries had done much good in Tahiti.
From a mountain, Darwin saw a ring of coral around a nearby island.
On 26 November 1835, the Beagle left Tahiti and sailed to New Zealand.
In December 1835, the Beagle reached the Bay of Islands in New Zealand.
Darwin met Maori men with beautiful patterns cut into their faces.
Darwin walked to a farm run by English missionaries in the bush.
In one rough town, Darwin saw sailors drinking and fighting in the streets.
On 30 December 1835, the Beagle left New Zealand, and Darwin was glad.
In January 1836, the Beagle reached Sydney, and Darwin admired the young city.
Darwin rode across the Blue Mountains and noticed the strange gum trees.
Darwin watched a platypus in a pond and thought about it for hours.
One night, Darwin watched Aboriginal people dance around a fire.
In February 1836, the Beagle reached Hobart, a town below a tall mountain.
In April 1836, the Beagle reached the Keeling Islands, a ring of palms.
Big waves crashed on the outer reef, but the living coral stayed strong.
Darwin learned about a giant crab that opens coconuts with its claws.
Darwin worked out that coral rings grow while an island slowly sinks.
At Mauritius, a kind officer welcomed Darwin, and he saw sugar fields.
At Cape Town, Darwin met the famous scientist Sir John Herschel.
At St Helena, Darwin visited the grave of Napoleon.
At Ascension, Darwin read letters saying his work was admired in England.
Darwin wanted to go home, but the ship had to return to Brazil.
The Beagle sailed to the Azores and then north toward England.
On 2 October 1836, the Beagle came into Falmouth, in England.
Darwin took a coach north and reached Shrewsbury late at night.
Next morning, Darwin walked in at breakfast and surprised his family.
Darwin gave his fossils and birds to experts to study.
Gould told Darwin that the small birds from the Galápagos were many kinds.
In 1837, Darwin began secret notebooks about how species change.
In 1838, Darwin read a book that gave him a big idea.
In 1839, Darwin published his diary of the voyage, and many people read it.
Later, the Beagle became a watch ship, and workers broke her up in 1870.
Darwin said the voyage was the most important event in his life.
B1B2: Charles Darwin was born in 1809 in Shrewsbury, a market town in the west of England. Instead of working hard at school, he spent his free hours collecting beetles, shells and birds' eggs.

At Cambridge he was supposed to prepare for life as a clergyman, but he liked beetles much more than books. Once, with a beetle in each hand, he put a third in his mouth, and it burned his tongue with a bitter liquid.
At Cambridge, Professor John Henslow became Darwin's teacher and close friend. He taught Darwin to look closely at nature, and to write down exactly what he saw.
In August 1831 Darwin went to Wales with Adam Sedgwick, a famous geologist. Together they tapped at rocks with hammers, and Darwin learned how the layers of stone tell the story of the past.

When Darwin came home from Wales, a letter from Henslow was waiting for him. It said that Captain FitzRoy needed a gentleman naturalist to sail round the world, and that other men had already refused.
Darwin's father, Dr Robert Darwin, did not like the idea at all. He thought the voyage would be a dangerous waste of time for a young man who was meant to become a clergyman.
However, Darwin's uncle, Josiah Wedgwood, wrote an answer to each of the father's worries. He then drove Darwin to Shrewsbury himself, and after they talked, Dr Darwin agreed to pay for the trip.

In September 1831 Darwin met Captain Robert FitzRoy in London. The captain believed that a person's face shows his character, and he almost refused Darwin because he did not like the shape of his nose.
The Beagle was a small ship, about twenty-seven metres long, and she was made ready at Plymouth. Darwin bought a microscope, a gun, jars for his specimens and a heavy geological hammer.
Strong winds twice forced the Beagle back into port, and Darwin began to feel ill with worry. At last, on 27 December 1831, the ship sailed from Devonport with the young naturalist on board.
As soon as the Beagle reached rough water, Darwin was terribly seasick. He found that the only thing that helped was lying flat in his hammock and eating dry biscuits and raisins.
Darwin shared the small cabin at the back of the ship with two young officers. He slept in a hammock above the chart table, and there was hardly room to stand.

About seventy people lived and worked on the Beagle, from the captain to the cabin boys. In time a young crew member, Syms Covington, became Darwin's helper, and he learned to skin birds and pack specimens.
Darwin and FitzRoy ate dinner together at the captain's small table every evening. The captain was hot-tempered and often lonely, but the two men slowly became good friends.

Soon the Beagle reached Tenerife, but the officials feared that the ship might carry cholera from England. They ordered a long quarantine, so the Beagle sailed on, and Darwin never saw the island he had longed to visit.
At Porto Praya on the island of St Jago, Darwin took his first walk on tropical land. The ground was black volcanic rock, the sun was fierce, and everything seemed strange and new.
In a sea cliff Darwin saw a white band of shells, high above the water. Lyell's book told him how to read such signs, and Darwin began to think that he might write a book of his own.
Darwin watched a small octopus in a rock pool, and saw it change colour like a cloud passing over. He also towed a fine net behind the ship, and in it he found many tiny, strange sea creatures.

St Paul's Rocks are small bare islands in the middle of the Atlantic, without a single tree. The only land animals were insects and spiders that lived on the seabirds, which hardly moved when the sailors came close.
Next came Fernando de Noronha, a volcanic island that Brazil used as a prison. Darwin saw a tall, strange rock rising from the forest, and he knew that Brazil was only a few days away.

On 28 February 1832 the Beagle reached Bahia, a Brazilian port with white churches among the palm trees. Darwin was so eager to see the tropics that he could hardly wait for the boat to reach the shore.
Darwin took his first walk in a tropical forest, and it was everything he had dreamed of. The leaves were huge, the flowers were brilliant, and he wrote that his mind was a chaos of delight.
On warm nights the sea around the Beagle glowed with a pale green light. Darwin looked closely at the water, and found that it was full of tiny living things that sparkled like stars.

On 4 April 1832 the Beagle sailed into the bay of Rio de Janeiro, with its strange Sugar Loaf mountain. Darwin found a small cottage near the shore, where he could keep his specimens and work in peace.
Darwin was invited to join an English party who were riding to the Rio Macaé, far to the north. They rode through forests and villages, and they stayed in simple inns where the food was plain.
On the ride Darwin collected beetles, butterflies and orchids, and he filled his boxes every night. After dark he lay awake listening to the frogs and insects, which sang as loudly as a crowd.

In the forest Darwin watched armies of small ants marching in long, wide lines across the ground. Spiders, cockroaches and other creatures ran away from them in terror, and he found it strange to watch.

On one plantation Darwin heard an angry master threaten to sell the families of his slaves, each one apart from the others. Darwin was horrified, and the thought of it made his blood boil for years afterward.

At the captain's table, Darwin said that the answers of slaves, given in front of their master, could not be trusted. FitzRoy flew into a rage, and said that they could not live together if Darwin doubted his word.
FitzRoy apologised the next day, and the two men made peace, so Darwin could stay in his cabin. In July 1832 the Beagle left Rio, and Darwin hoped that slavery would one day come to an end.
In July 1832 the Beagle reached Montevideo, on the wide, muddy River Plate. FitzRoy was going to survey the coast for months, so Darwin planned to spend that time exploring on land.
At the small town of Maldonado, Darwin stayed in a simple house for several weeks. There he collected birds, snakes and small animals, and he learned how to prepare each one for the boxes.

Darwin saw the capybara, which is the largest rodent in the world, resting beside a stream. He also heard the strange cry of a small animal called the tucotuco, which lives in burrows underground and is rarely seen.

In September 1832 the Beagle reached Bahía Blanca, a lonely stretch of mud flats and low cliffs on the coast of Argentina. While the sailors surveyed, Darwin walked along the shore at Punta Alta to see what the cliffs held.
In a low cliff at Punta Alta, Darwin noticed some huge bones and teeth sticking out of the earth. He had never seen anything like them, and he could not tell what animals they came from.
He returned to the cliff day after day and dug out a great skull and many other bones. Because they were old and easily broken, he wrapped each one carefully in paper and cloth.

The bones belonged to giant animals that no longer live anywhere on Earth, including ground sloths as big as elephants. Some were relatives of the sloth and the armadillo, but they were far larger than any living member of those families.
In the same cliff Darwin found the tooth of a horse, which puzzled him greatly. There were no horses in America when the Spaniards arrived, yet here was a tooth from a horse that had died long ago.

Darwin noticed that the extinct giants of this land were like the small animals that still live in South America, such as the armadillo. He asked himself why the old animals and the new ones of the same place should be so alike.
Darwin packed the bones carefully, wrote notes for each one and sent them to Professor Henslow in Cambridge. He hoped that his old teacher would take good care of them until he came home.
In December 1832 the Beagle sailed south from the River Plate, toward the cold tip of South America. On board were three Fuegians whom FitzRoy meant to take back to their homes.

On 18 December the Beagle anchored in Good Success Bay, in Tierra del Fuego, below dark hills and forest. Darwin saw his first Fuegians, who stood on a headland and shouted and waved their arms at the ship.

The Fuegians watched the sailors carefully, and copied their words and movements so well that Darwin was astonished. If a sailor yawned or coughed, the Fuegians did the same, and they could even repeat whole sentences in English.

On a cold day, sleet fell on a Fuegian woman who sat in a canoe by the ship, nursing her baby. The sleet melted on the bare skin of both mother and child, yet they did not seem to mind, and Darwin was amazed.
In January 1833, while the Beagle was trying to sail round Cape Horn, a huge wave crashed over the deck. It smashed one of the boats, and for a moment the ship seemed to be in great danger.

FitzRoy had taken the three Fuegians to England in 1830, and there they had learned English and some English manners. Jemmy Button was a boy, York Minster was a strong man and Fuegia Basket was a girl, and all three had met the King.

Jemmy Button was cheerful, neat and rather vain, and he liked to keep his leather shoes clean and shiny. He was kind-hearted, too, and he felt sorry for sailors who were seasick, though he found it a little funny.

At a bay called Woollya, FitzRoy's men built three wooden huts and planted a garden. They had brought many things for the new settlement, including tea sets and fine white linen, which were of little use in such a place.

Jemmy met his mother and brothers on the beach, but he had forgotten much of his own language and felt strange among them. Many Fuegians came to stare at the visitors, and they took anything that they could carry away.

After about ten days the Beagle sailed away to survey the coast, and she returned a month later to see how the settlers were. Richard Matthews had been robbed and was frightened, so FitzRoy decided to take him back on board.

In March 1833 the Beagle reached the Falkland Islands, a cold and windy group of islands without a single tree. Wild cattle and horses roamed over the brown hills, and the few settlers lived in poor houses beside the sea.
In the Falklands Darwin met a wild fox that was not afraid of people. He wrote that it would probably disappear once people settled the islands, and sadly it did, in the 1870s.

In the valleys of the Falklands, Darwin saw long streams of huge grey stones that ran down the slopes like frozen rivers. He wondered how they had been made, because no water flowed through them, and the puzzle stayed with him for a long time.

In August 1833 the Beagle reached the Río Negro, and Darwin decided to travel overland to Buenos Aires instead of staying on the ship. It was a ride of hundreds of miles across wild country, and he took only a few guides and horses.

On the pampas Darwin rode all day with the gauchos, the horsemen of the plains. They roasted beef on long spears over a fire, drank a bitter tea called mate, and slept on the ground with their saddles for pillows.

At the Colorado River Darwin visited the large camp of General Rosas, who was leading an army against the Indians of the plains. Rosas gave him a passport that allowed him to use the horses at the post houses along the way.
Darwin was shocked by the war against the Indians, in which families were hunted and many were killed. He wrote that it was hard to believe that such cruel acts could be done in a Christian country.

The gauchos used ropes with heavy balls, called bolas, to catch animals. Darwin tried one himself, but the ropes wrapped around his own horse's legs, and the gauchos laughed until they could hardly stand.
At night the gauchos cooked an armadillo in its own shell, over the glowing coals of the fire. The Spanish say that this makes meat and dish in one, and Darwin thought it tasted very good.

After many days in the saddle, with stops at lonely post houses to change horses, Darwin reached Buenos Aires in September 1833. He had ridden hundreds of miles across the pampas, and he had learned much about the life of the plains.
From Buenos Aires Darwin travelled north to Santa Fe, partly by river and partly on horseback. He crossed the great Paraná river in a small boat, while his horses swam beside him.
In the red cliffs beside the Paraná, Darwin found layers of sea shells and the bones of ancient animals. They showed that the sea had once covered the land, and that the land had since risen.

On the plains Darwin saw thistles that were taller than his horse, growing in thick masses for many miles. They had come from Europe, and they had spread so fast that they had crowded out the native plants.
At a farm in Uruguay, near the Río Negro, Darwin heard of a huge skull that the farmer kept. He bought it for eighteen pence, and it later proved to belong to a giant animal now called Toxodon.
Darwin also found pieces of a huge shell made of many small plates fitted together. A farmer told him that it came from a giant armadillo, and experts later named the animal Glyptodon.

Darwin asked himself why such giant animals had died out. He decided that we should not be surprised, because a rare kind of animal grows rarer before it vanishes, just as sickness comes before death.

Off the coast of Argentina, countless white and yellow butterflies flew around the Beagle until the ropes looked as if they were covered with snow. Darwin watched the living cloud for a long time, and he wondered how such delicate creatures could travel so far over the sea.
Every day Darwin wrote in his diary, and he kept a list of every specimen with a number. Whenever a ship sailed for England, he sent a box of specimens and a long letter home.
On the plains Darwin slept in the open air with a saddle for a pillow and a horse-cloth for a bed. Looking up at the huge, starry sky, he felt wonderfully free.
In November 1833 Darwin rejoined the Beagle at Montevideo, bringing his boxes of bones and animals. FitzRoy was already preparing to sail south again, and the coast of Patagonia lay ahead of them.
Patagonia is a wide, dry land of gravel and thorny bushes, with hardly any water. People called these plains useless, but Darwin found that they stayed in his mind for years.

Guanacos, which are wild cousins of the llama, stood on the hills and watched the travellers with long, graceful necks. They are so curious that if a man lies on the ground and waves his legs, they will come closer to look.

At Christmas Darwin and his friends enjoyed a dinner of roast rhea, a large bird like an ostrich. Only when it was half eaten did Darwin see that it was the rarer, smaller kind, and he saved the head and legs.
Darwin ate puma meat for the first time, and found it white and rather like veal. He also learned that the puma, which lives alone, hunts the guanacos and is the great enemy of the plains.
Next the Beagle stopped at Port St Julian, a harbour where Magellan had spent the winter in 1520. His captains had rebelled there, and the explorer had to crush the mutiny before sailing on.
Near Port St Julian, Darwin found the bones of a giant animal with a long neck that looked like a huge llama. It was later named Macrauchenia, and it had been as big as a camel.

Darwin saw that the plains of Patagonia rise in a series of great steps, covered with round pebbles. He realised that each step was an old beach, and that the whole land had been lifted from the sea in stages.
A condor soared above the cliffs on wings about three metres wide. Darwin watched it for half an hour and never saw it flap its wings once.
Darwin noticed that guanacos seem to go to the same places beside the rivers to die. In some of these places the ground was white with bones.
Darwin learned that Patagonia has two kinds of rhea, and that they live in different regions. The common kind lives in the north and the smaller kind in the south, and he wondered why.
In early 1834 the Beagle entered the Beagle Channel again, a long strait between steep forests and snowy mountains. Darwin thought it as wild and beautiful as any place on the whole voyage.
