In the channel Darwin saw forests of giant kelp, a seaweed that grows many metres long in the cold water. He wrote that thousands of animals live among its leaves, and that if the kelp died, they would all die with it.
Where the glaciers met the sea, great blue cliffs of ice rose above the water. One day a huge piece broke off and made a wave that nearly wrecked the boats, until the men pulled them up the beach.
Darwin watched the Fuegians who lived by the shore, travelling in canoes with their families. They lived on shellfish, seals and berries, and they slept in simple shelters made of branches.

A year after the first visit, the Beagle returned to Woollya, and a thin man in a canoe came out to meet the boat. It was Jemmy Button, with long hair and only a blanket round his waist, and Darwin had never seen such a sad change.

That evening Jemmy dined with FitzRoy, and ate as neatly with his knife and fork as he had done before. He brought presents of otter skins and spears, and he said that he was happy and did not want to go back to England.

When the Beagle sailed away, Jemmy lit a great fire on the shore as a farewell signal, and the smoke rose into the sky. Darwin heard that York Minster had robbed Jemmy of his goods and gone away with Fuegia Basket.
In the beech forests Darwin saw round yellow fungi that grew in bunches on the trunks of the trees. The Fuegians ate them, and they were almost the only food from the forest besides berries.

From the Strait of Magellan Darwin saw Mount Sarmiento, a huge cone of ice and snow rising straight from the sea. He thought it one of the grandest sights of the whole voyage, especially when the clouds lifted.
Back in the Falkland Islands, Darwin watched jackass penguins, which stand upright on the shore like little men. They bray like donkeys on land, but in the water they dive and swim as fast as fish.
At Santa Cruz the crew pulled the Beagle onto the beach at high tide, so that they could repair and clean her. Meanwhile FitzRoy began to plan a bold trip up the river, toward the distant Andes.
FitzRoy, Darwin and about twenty-five men set off in three whaleboats to explore the Santa Cruz River. They took food for three weeks, and nobody knew how far the river would lead them.

The current was too strong for rowing, so the men walked along the bank and pulled the boats with long ropes. Darwin helped with the ropes, and in the evenings the party cooked guanaco meat over a fire on the stony shore.

The river ran through a flat, dry plain, between cliffs of black volcanic rock called basalt. Its water was a milky blue colour, and its bed was full of stones that had been carried down from the Andes.

After about two weeks, the party saw the snowy peaks of the Andes far away on the horizon. By then half the food was gone, and FitzRoy decided that they must turn back, even though the mountains were still a long way off.

Going home was easy, because the current carried the boats downstream almost without help. They covered in a few days the distance that had taken them more than two weeks, and they were soon back aboard the Beagle.
The Beagle then sailed into the Strait of Magellan and reached Port Famine. An English sailor gave the harbour that name in 1587, after he found a Spanish colony where almost everyone had starved.

Darwin climbed Mount Tarn, a mountain about eight hundred metres high, through thick beech forest and then over snow. From the top he looked over a wild land of mountains, channels and glaciers, and he felt very small.

In June 1834 the Beagle finally left the Strait and entered the Pacific Ocean, with huge swells rolling under her. After so many months in cold and rain, the crew looked forward to the warm sun and the green valleys of Chile.

On 23 July 1834 the Beagle reached Valparaíso, in Chile, where white houses climb steep brown hills beneath the Andes. Darwin was delighted to meet his old school friend Richard Corfield, who was now a merchant there.
After the grey, wet south, Chile seemed bright and dry, with brown hills, tall cactus and warm sunshine. Darwin felt that life had begun again, and he could hardly wait to explore the country.

In August 1834 Darwin hired a guide named Mariano Gonzales and ten mules, and set out to explore the country. The mules followed a mare with a little bell round her neck, and they would not stray from her.
Darwin rode over dry hills and through green valleys to Santiago, the capital of Chile. From there he went south to the mining country, sleeping each night wherever the day's ride ended.
In a copper mine Darwin saw the miners climb steep ladders with enormous loads of ore on their backs. He was amazed at their strength, and shocked that such hard work earned them so little.
In the country of Chile, farmers welcomed Darwin warmly and gave him food and a bed for the night. They often refused to take any payment, and he was touched by their kindness.
From Santiago Darwin could see the Andes, with their snowy peaks glowing pink in the evening light. He had already begun to dream of crossing them, and the idea grew stronger every day.
On the hills near the coast Darwin found sea shells in the rock, far above the level of the sea. He realised that the coast of Chile had been lifted up, just as Lyell had suggested.
In late September 1834 Darwin returned to Valparaíso and fell ill with a fever. It was probably caused by bad food or water, and he was soon too weak to leave his bed.
Richard Corfield looked after Darwin in his own house, and Darwin stayed in bed for about a month. While he got better, he thought about all he had seen and wrote long letters to his family.
On 10 November 1834 the Beagle left Valparaíso for the south. Darwin was still thin and pale, but he was strong enough to travel, and he was happy to be with his friends again.
The Beagle sailed to the island of Chiloé, a rainy land of thick green forest and small villages. It rained almost every day, but Darwin found the dark forests beautiful.
At Chiloé a small dark fox sat on the rocks, so busy watching the surveyors that Darwin was able to walk right up to it. It turned out to be a new kind of fox, which is now called Darwin's fox.
The forests of Chiloé were so thick that Darwin could hardly move through them. The ground was covered with fallen trunks, bamboo and giant ferns, so he often had to climb along the trees.

Darwin rode to Castro, the old capital of the island, which was a quiet town of wooden houses with grass growing in the streets. The people were poor, but they were friendly, and they welcomed the strangers to their homes.
The Chilotes cooked their food in a hole in the ground, with hot stones, leaves, shellfish, potatoes and pork all piled together. Darwin watched them and tasted the meal, which was simple but good.

In the nearby Chonos Islands Darwin found wild potatoes growing on the sandy beaches. He knew that these plants were relatives of the potatoes grown in Europe, and that the potato comes from this part of the world.

On 19 January 1835 Darwin saw the volcano Osorno burst into eruption in the night, a red glow in the sky above the dark sea. Showers of burning rocks shot up from the top and then fell again, like fireworks.

Darwin later learned that two other volcanoes had erupted at almost the same time, one in the Andes and one far away in Nicaragua. He began to suspect that volcanoes are connected deep under the ground.
In February 1835 the Beagle reached Valdivia, a small town surrounded by thick forest and famous for its apples. The country seemed peaceful and green, and Darwin was looking forward to a quiet week.
Darwin walked through the orchards of Valdivia, where the branches bent under the weight of apples. The people made cider from them, and he had no idea what the next day would bring.
On 20 February 1835 Darwin was resting on the ground in a forest near Valdivia, when a powerful earthquake shook the land. The ground rolled like waves, and the trees swayed above him.
The earthquake lasted about two minutes, and Darwin could hardly keep his balance. He said that it felt like walking on thin ice that bends under your feet.
Darwin wrote that an earthquake destroys our oldest ideas in a moment. The earth, which we think of as the very symbol of safety, had moved under his feet like a thin crust over a liquid.
At Valdivia the damage was small, and the people were only frightened. But the sea behaved strangely, and soon news came that the city of Concepción had suffered terribly.
On 4 March 1835 the Beagle reached Concepción and the nearby port of Talcahuano. Both towns lay in ruins, and the shore was covered with timber and furniture, as if a thousand ships had been wrecked.
Most of the people had escaped with their lives, because the shock was slow enough to let them run out of their houses. Darwin knew that if it had happened at night, many more would have died.

After the shaking stopped, a great wave rolled in from the sea and swept over the shore, carrying boats, timber and furniture far inland. Darwin heard that the water had first drawn back from the coast, and then returned with terrible force.

Darwin and FitzRoy measured the shore and found that the land near Concepción had risen by two or three feet. Beds of mussels that had once lived under water were now dead and dry, and they lay far above the tide.
At Santa Maria island the land had risen about three metres at one end. Darwin walked over old mussel beds and rotting shells that were now high above the reach of the waves.

Darwin concluded that earthquakes and volcanoes come from the same cause, deep inside the earth. The land rises by small jerks during earthquakes, and this, he thought, was how mountain ranges were built.
In March 1835 Darwin returned to Santiago and set out again with Mariano Gonzales and a train of mules. His plan was to cross the Andes, the huge mountain range between Chile and Argentina.
The party followed a deep valley with steep cliffs on both sides and a loud river far below. The path was narrow, and the mules stepped carefully along the edge of the drop.
Near the top, the snow lay deep, and the line of mules and men slowly crossed the high pass of Portillo. The air was thin and cold, and the peaks around them were white against a dark blue sky.
In a cliff near the highest pass, Darwin found fossil seashells in the rock, more than 3,500 metres above the sea. He knew at once that this high land must once have been under the ocean.
From the highest pass Darwin looked east over a plain that was as flat and wide as the sea. He also noticed that the plants and insects on the two sides of the mountains were quite different.
In the thin air Darwin gasped for breath, and his mules stopped often to rest. His guide blamed the snow, but Darwin thought that the real cause was the height.
East of the mountains Darwin reached Mendoza, a town of vineyards, fig trees and peaches on a dry plain. After the hard climb, he enjoyed good fruit and rest in the warm sun.
At the village of Luxan, a blood-sucking bug called the benchuca bit Darwin in the night. Some scientists think it may have given him a lasting illness, though this is still debated.

On the way back Darwin crossed the Uspallata pass and found a group of trees that had turned to stone. They stood upright, and they showed that the land there had once been low, and had later been lifted high.
Darwin concluded that the Andes were raised bit by bit over a very long time. Lyell had taught that small changes could add up to great ones, and now Darwin had seen the proof with his own eyes.
Darwin rejoined the Beagle, which sailed north along a brown and dry coast where almost nothing grew. For hundreds of miles there was hardly a tree, and the mountains rose bare from the sea.
In June 1835 Darwin rode to Copiapó through desert valleys where rain falls very rarely. Farms could only grow beside the little rivers, and a few miles away the land was completely dry.
At Iquique there was no fresh water at all, so it had to be brought in by boat from another town. Darwin visited the nitre works on the plain, where the earth was dug up to make fertiliser.
In July 1835 the Beagle reached Callao, the port of Lima, in Peru. A grey mist hung over the city, and rain hardly ever fell, so the land around it was dusty and dull.
Darwin saw that the women of Lima wore black veils that covered everything except one eye. He found the city dirty and sad, though it had once been rich and grand.

Near Callao Darwin saw the ruins of the old port, which was destroyed in 1746 by an earthquake and a great sea wave. The wave had thrown ships far inland, and the broken walls were still standing in the sand.

On the island of San Lorenzo, Darwin found sea shells about twenty-five metres above the water. Among the shells he even found pieces of string and corn, which meant that the land had risen since people lived on the coast.

FitzRoy had more than twenty chronometers on board, and he checked them often against the stars. He wanted to measure the distance round the whole world as exactly as possible, and Darwin admired his patience.

On 7 September 1835 the Beagle left Peru and sailed west across the open Pacific, toward the Galápagos Islands. Darwin watched the empty sea and looked forward to a place of which he knew very little.

On 15 September 1835 the crew sighted the Galápagos Islands, a group of black volcanic islands on the equator. They saw low hills, bare slopes and small cones, and no one on board knew what strange creatures lived there.

On Chatham Island, the first of the Galápagos that Darwin visited, the ground was hot black lava covered with bushes that had no leaves. It was a strange and silent place, and Darwin thought it looked like a land from another world.
Darwin watched the sea lizards, called marine iguanas, which swim in the cold sea and eat seaweed. He thought them ugly and called them imps of darkness, but he was fascinated by how they lived.
On James Island Darwin camped for several days with a few men. The land was full of yellow land iguanas, and there were so many burrows that it was hard to find a place for the tent.

The sailors took live tortoises on board the Beagle, because the animals can live for months without food and give fresh meat. So many had been taken over the years that they were becoming rare on some of the islands.

The animals of the Galápagos had never learned to fear people, and they were wonderfully tame. Darwin once pushed a hawk off a branch with the end of his gun, and a mockingbird drank water from a pitcher in his hand.

In late October 1835 the Beagle left the Galápagos and began a long voyage across the open Pacific. For more than three weeks there was no land at all, only blue water, flying fish and wide empty skies.

On 15 November 1835 the Beagle reached Tahiti, an island of high green mountains and white beaches. Darwin was delighted by the view from the ship, and he was impatient to go ashore.

Darwin set out inland with two guides, who carried food and water in tubes of bamboo. On the way they caught small fish in the stream with their hands, and they cooked them in leaves over hot stones.

The party climbed a cliff using ropes, and from the top they could see a valley full of waterfalls, tree ferns and fruit trees. That night they slept under a shelter of leaves, and the guides said a prayer before they lay down.
On Sunday Darwin went to a Tahitian church, where the people sat quietly in neat clothes. He was impressed by how orderly and attentive they were, though he could not understand the words.

Before the voyage Darwin had heard people say that the missionaries had spoiled Tahiti. After talking with the islanders, he believed that they had done much good, because the people had become more peaceful and honest.

From a high place Darwin saw the neighbouring island of Eimeo, ringed by a white line of surf. A reef lay all around it, with calm water inside, and this fitted his growing idea of how coral rings form.
On 26 November 1835 the Beagle left Tahiti and set sail for New Zealand. Darwin was seasick again, but he carried happy memories of the island and its people.

In December 1835 the Beagle reached the Bay of Islands in New Zealand, where Darwin saw an English mission among Maori villages. The little settlement had neat houses and gardens, and it seemed very strange to him in such a distant land.
Darwin met the Maori, a proud and energetic people who tattooed their faces with beautiful patterns. He thought them very different from the Fuegians, because they were strong, active and clever.

Darwin walked to Waimate, an English-style farm with hedges, wheat and flowers in the middle of the New Zealand bush. It was run by missionaries, and the sight of a quiet English farm in that wild land delighted him.
At Kororareka, a rough port town, Darwin saw sailors and settlers drinking and fighting in the streets. He was shocked by the bad behaviour of so many Englishmen so far from home.

On 30 December 1835 the Beagle left New Zealand, and Darwin wrote that all on board were glad to go. He found the country less pleasant than Tahiti, and he was looking forward to the warm sun of Australia.

In January 1836 the Beagle reached Sydney, a bright new town of stone houses and busy streets beside a beautiful harbour. Darwin was astonished that so fine a city could have grown in less than fifty years.
Darwin rode inland across the Blue Mountains with a guide. He noticed that the leaves of the gum trees hang edgeways, so that they give very little shade.

In the bush Darwin watched a platypus swimming in a quiet pond, and an ant-lion trapping ants in a sandy pit. The platypus was unlike other animals, but the ant-lion's pit was like those of Europe, and he wondered how many Creators there were.

One night Darwin watched a group of Aboriginal people dance by firelight, painted in white and moving to a strong beat. He wrote that wherever Europeans had settled, the Aboriginal people had suffered great harm.

In February 1836 the Beagle reached Hobart, in Van Diemen's Land, a pretty town below a tall mountain. Darwin learned that the island's Aboriginal people had been taken away by the settlers, and he thought it very sad.

In April 1836 the Beagle reached the Keeling Islands, a ring of coral and palm trees around a quiet lagoon. The islands were only a few metres above the sea, and Darwin wondered how they could have been built.

On the outer edge of the reef, huge waves crashed all day long, yet the living coral and pink seaweed held firm. Darwin admired how such small creatures could build a wall strong enough to stand against the ocean.
Darwin learned about the robber crab, a huge land crab that lives under the palm trees. The islanders told him that it climbs the trees and opens the coconuts with its strong claws.
Darwin worked out how a ring of coral islands forms. A volcanic island slowly sinks, while the coral on its edge keeps growing upward, until only a ring around a lagoon is left.
At Mauritius, an island in the Indian Ocean, a kind English officer welcomed Darwin into his home. He saw sugar fields and rough mountains, and he enjoyed some days of rest on land.

At Cape Town in South Africa, Darwin and FitzRoy visited the famous astronomer Sir John Herschel at his home. Darwin felt honoured to meet one of the great scientists of the age, whose books he had read.

At St Helena Darwin walked up to the grave of Napoleon, which lay under a willow tree in a quiet valley. He also saw that goats had eaten the island's original forest, and that most of its plants had been brought from other lands.
At Ascension Darwin found letters from home that made him very happy. They said that Henslow had read his notes to scientists at Cambridge, and that his collections were already admired.
To check his clocks, FitzRoy sailed back to Bahia, which was in the wrong direction. Darwin was furious at the delay, and he wrote that he hated the sea and was glad to leave Brazil forever.
The Beagle sailed on to the Azores, a group of green islands in the Atlantic, and then turned north toward England. Autumn storms rocked the ship, but Darwin could think only of home.
On 2 October 1836 the Beagle came into Falmouth, in the south-west of England, after four years and nine months. Darwin was not sorry to leave the ship, and he hurried to find a coach for home.
Darwin travelled north by coach for two days and reached Shrewsbury late at night on 4 October. He went quietly to bed in the house where he had grown up.
The next morning Darwin walked into the breakfast room, to the great surprise of his sisters and his father. Dr Darwin looked at him closely, and said that the shape of his head had altered.
Darwin gave his fossils to Richard Owen, and his birds to John Gould, who were experts in their subjects. They worked for months to name the animals, and the results surprised everyone.

In 1837 Gould told Darwin that the small birds from the Galápagos were a group of many related kinds. The mockingbirds were different on each island, too, so Darwin asked FitzRoy and others to share their labels.
In 1837 Darwin began secret notebooks about how species change. On one page he drew a small tree with branches, to show how new kinds might grow from old ones.

In 1838 Darwin read a famous essay on population by Thomas Malthus, and it gave him an important idea. He saw that in the struggle for life the best-fitted animals would survive, and he later explained this in On the Origin of Species.
In 1839 Darwin published the story of his journey, and it soon became a popular book. Later readers called it The Voyage of the Beagle, and many have loved it ever since.
The Beagle made one more long survey voyage, and then she became a watch ship on the coast of England. In 1870 she was sold and broken up, but her name is now famous all over the world.

Darwin later said that the voyage was the most important event of his life, because it decided his whole career. FitzRoy, too, found a new calling, and he helped to start weather forecasting in Britain.

When Darwin came home from Wales he found a letter waiting from Henslow, and it was to change the course of his life. Several other men had already refused, including Henslow himself, and Darwin's heart leapt at the thought.

Dr Robert Darwin, a large and careful man, did not like the plan at all, and he listed his objections one by one. He feared that it would look badly for a young man who had already given up medicine, and that the voyage would be a useless waste of time and an uncomfortable danger. Yet he added that if any sensible person advised Darwin to go, he would give his consent.

Darwin's uncle, Josiah Wedgwood, whom the family trusted for his good sense, wrote a careful reply to each of the doctor's objections. Dr Darwin listened, gave way at last and promised to pay for his son's voyage, and Darwin rushed off to tell his friends.

FitzRoy believed in reading a man's character from his face, and he doubted that anyone with Darwin's nose could have the energy for such a voyage. Fortunately the two took to one another during their talk, and the captain chose him.

Anxious and excited by turns, he wondered whether he would be equal to the task.

At last, on 27 December 1831, the little ship slipped out of Devonport harbour under grey clouds. Ahead of her lay almost five years, and Darwin could not have guessed how much of the world he would see.

The Beagle had hardly left the shelter of the land before the swell caught her, and Darwin discovered that he was a wretched sailor. He lay flat in his hammock for hours, nibbling dry biscuits and raisins, and wondering whether he had made a terrible mistake. The poop cabin, where Darwin lived and worked, was scarcely larger than a cupboard and had to be shared with two young officers. Everywhere were gigantic leaves, flowers of dazzling colour, climbing plants as thick as ropes and butterflies drifting through the shade. His mind, he wrote, was a chaos of delight, and he knew that the memory would stay with him for the rest of his life.

At night in the warm tropical sea the water around the Beagle began to glow, and in the wake of the ship a pale green fire rolled away across the darkness. Darwin scooped up some of the sea in a jar, and under his lens he found that it was full of tiny living creatures that gave off the light. It was a wonder that made the whole ocean seem alive, and he added it to the long list of things he meant to understand.

When the Spaniards arrived in America there had been no horses there at all, yet here was a tooth from a horse that had lived and died long before. It seemed marvellous to him that a wild horse had once roamed the continent, vanished, and then returned in the ships of Europe to multiply across the plains.

Darwin began to see a pattern that caught at his thoughts: the extinct giants of this land were cousins of the small animals that still live in South America today. The great sloth resembled the living sloths, and the monstrous armoured creature looked like an armadillo of enormous size. Why, he asked himself, should the dead and the living of a single place be so alike?

Darwin packed the bones with the greatest care, wrote notes about where each had lain and sent the cases to his old teacher, Professor Henslow, at Cambridge. He knew that he could trust Henslow to look after them, and he hoped that his friend would be pleased with so strange a gift. Months would pass before an answer reached him, and in the meantime the Beagle sailed on.

If a sailor coughed or yawned, they coughed and yawned too, and they could repeat whole sentences of English after hearing them only once. Darwin found the scenery bleak, but he was glad to be on land again, and he set off to see what the islands contained.

He remarked that such a fearless animal would not survive once the islands filled with people, and he predicted that it would soon vanish. No water moved through them, and no one could say how such tumbled rivers of stone had formed. It was a puzzle that he turned over in his mind for a long time, as he did with every mystery of the land.
