It was a ride of hundreds of miles across wild country, with a few guides, spare horses and almost no baggage, and he set out with a light heart. FitzRoy would continue the survey by sea, and the two were to meet again some months later.

On the pampas Darwin rode all day with the gauchos, the proud and hardy horsemen of the plains, who treated him with grave politeness. At night they roasted beef on long spears over a fire, drank a bitter tea called mate, and lay down on the bare ground with their saddles for pillows. Darwin, wrapped in a poncho and looking up at the stars, discovered that he liked this life.

At the Colorado River Darwin visited the great camp of General Rosas, a strong and feared man who was leading an army against the Indians of the plains. The general received him with courtesy and gave him a passport which allowed him to use the horses kept at the post houses along the way. Without that piece of paper, his journey would have been far slower, and perhaps impossible.

Darwin was shocked by the war that Rosas was waging, in which whole families of Indians were hunted down and many of them killed. He wrote that it was hard to believe such cruelty could take place in a Christian country, and that the soldiers called it justice because their enemies were savages. For all his love of adventure, he left the camp with a heavy heart.

The gauchos used a weapon called the bolas, a set of heavy balls joined by cords, which they threw to tangle the legs of horses and cattle. Darwin was determined to try it for himself, and one day he whirled the balls above his head and let them fly. The cords wrapped around his own horse's legs, and down it went, while the gauchos roared with laughter.

In the evenings the gauchos cooked an armadillo in its own shell, setting it on the glowing coals of the fire. The Spanish say that this makes meat and dish in one, and Darwin found the flesh so good that he ate it with real pleasure. After many meals of plain beef it was a welcome change, and the horsemen watched with approval as the stranger enjoyed their food.

After many days in the saddle, stopping at lonely post houses to change horses and snatch a meal, Darwin reached Buenos Aires in September 1833. He had ridden hundreds of miles across the pampas, past herds of wild cattle and flocks of rheas, and he had learned more about the life of the plains than any book could teach. The adventure had given him a taste for travel on land that he would never lose.

From Buenos Aires Darwin travelled north to the city of Santa Fe, partly by river and partly on horseback, still hungry for fossils and for adventure. At the great Paraná he and his guides crossed in a small boat while their horses swam alongside, their heads held above the brown water. On the far side lay a country of low cliffs, wide marshes and endless grass, and he looked forward eagerly to the days to come.

In the red cliffs beside the Paraná Darwin found layers of sea shells lying above layers of ancient mud, and among them the bones of huge extinct animals. The shells proved that the sea had once covered the whole region, and the bones showed that great beasts had walked over the land after it rose. He wrote down every measurement and every detail, for he sensed that these cliffs held a long story and that he had only begun to read it.

On the plains Darwin rode through thickets of giant thistles as high as a horse's back, which covered whole districts for mile after mile. They had come from Europe, and they had spread so fast that they had crowded out the native plants and made the land almost impassable. It was a vivid lesson in how quickly one kind of plant can conquer a country when conditions are in its favour.

At a farm in Uruguay, near the Río Negro, Darwin heard of an enormous skull that the farmer had kept for years in his house. He bought it for eighteen pence, and it proved to be the head of Toxodon, a huge and strange beast which the experts could not easily classify. It was one of the most remarkable fossils of his whole journey, and he carried it back with the greatest care.

Darwin also found fragments of a huge, curved shell made of many small plates fitted together like stone tiles. A farmer told him that it had come from a giant armadillo, and he was right, for experts later named the creature Glyptodon, a great armoured animal about the size of a small car. Once again Darwin was struck that the extinct giant resembled a small animal still living in the same country.

Darwin often asked himself why such huge animals had vanished from the plains, and he refused to believe in some sudden and mysterious catastrophe. A kind of animal, he reasoned, always becomes rarer before it disappears, and we feel no surprise at the sickness of a creature, yet we marvel when it finally dies. In the same way, it was natural that the giants of South America should have faded away, even if the exact causes were hidden.

Off the coast of Argentina the Beagle sailed through a cloud of butterflies, thousands upon thousands of them, so thick in the air that the ropes and sails seemed to be covered with snow. Darwin watched the shimmering mass for hours, marvelling that such fragile creatures could survive so far from the land. It was one more wonder that he noted in the diary he kept so faithfully.

Every day Darwin wrote in his diary, and he kept a numbered list of every specimen so that nothing should be lost or confused. Whenever a ship sailed for England he sent home a box of specimens together with a long letter to Henslow or to his family. This steady and patient habit was the secret of his success, for it turned a wandering traveller into a scientist.

Night after night on the plains Darwin lay in the open air, with a saddle for a pillow and a rough cloth for a bed, and looked up at the great southern sky. The stars shone with a brilliance that he had never seen in England, and the Southern Cross hung low above the dark horizon. He felt wonderfully free, and he knew that he would remember these nights for the rest of his life.

In November 1833 Darwin rejoined the Beagle at Montevideo, bringing with him a rich load of bones, skins and notes from the pampas. FitzRoy was already preparing to sail south again, and the long, empty coast of Patagonia lay before them. Darwin had ridden and boated for months, and he was glad to find letters from home waiting in his cabin.

Patagonia, to most people, was a wretched wilderness of gravel, thorn and silence, and Darwin himself found little to love in its plains. Yet he discovered, to his surprise, that these empty stretches fixed themselves in his memory more firmly than the forests of Brazil and the glories of the tropics. He wondered why this was so, and decided that it was the great vacancy of the place, which gave the mind room to imagine without limit.

On the dry plains Darwin saw herds of guanacos, the graceful wild cousins of the llama, standing on the ridges with their long necks raised to watch the strangers. They were such curious animals that if a man lay on the ground and kicked his legs in the air, they would come closer to see what was happening. Their shrill neigh of alarm carried far over the plain, and they would then run off in a graceful line.

At Christmas the party sat round a fire to a feast of roast rhea, and the great bird was soon reduced to bones. Only when half of it had been eaten did Darwin realise that this was no common rhea but the rarer, smaller kind that the local people called petise, which he had long been hoping to find. He rescued the head, the neck, the legs and the larger feathers, and from these remains the animal was later named in his honour.

For the first time Darwin tasted puma meat, and he found it pale and not unlike veal, as the local people had said. He learned that the puma, a great solitary cat, is the chief enemy of the guanaco, and that it creeps up through the bushes to leap on its prey. The tracks of the hunter ran across the soft ground, and they reminded him that the plains were full of watchful life.

Next the Beagle put into Port St Julian, a bleak harbour where Magellan had spent the winter of 1520 during his famous voyage round the world. It was here that some of his captains had rebelled against him, and the great explorer had crushed the mutiny with ruthless speed. Darwin, strolling over the barren shore where such dramas had taken place, felt the weight of history lying quietly upon the land.

Near Port St Julian Darwin dug the bones of a great long-necked animal out of a cliff of gravel, and judged that it belonged to the llama family. It was later named Macrauchenia, and it had been as big as a camel, though experts found that in some features it resembled a rhinoceros or a tapir. Once again the dead giant belonged to a land where smaller cousins of the same family, the guanacos, still lived.

Everywhere along the coast Darwin saw that the plains of Patagonia rise in a series of great terraces, like gigantic stairs, each one covered with pebbles that had been rolled smooth by water. He realised that each step had once been a beach, and that the whole country had been lifted out of the sea, a little at a time, over an immense period. The idea fitted perfectly with what he had learned from Lyell and seen on St Jago, and it grew into one of the great themes of his geology.

Above the sea cliffs a condor floated on motionless wings, sweeping in long, slow circles that carried it higher without a single beat. Darwin, who judged that the bird measured about three metres from wing tip to wing tip, watched it for half an hour and never once saw it flap. It seemed to him a perfect lesson in how an animal can master the air with almost no effort.

Darwin noticed that the guanacos of Patagonia seem to choose certain places beside the rivers to die, for in these spots the ground was white with their bones. Some of the sick or the old, he thought, must go to the water and lie down among the bushes, where they could drink until the end. He could not be sure, and he did not pretend to know, but he faithfully recorded what he saw.

From the local people and from his own observations Darwin learned that Patagonia has two kinds of rhea, which are alike in appearance but live in different regions. The common kind lives to the north and the smaller kind to the south, and near the Río Negro they meet, so that one replaces the other. He asked himself why two similar creatures should divide a country between them, and the question stayed with him.

In early 1834 the Beagle entered the Beagle Channel again, that long and narrow strait which winds between steep, forested slopes and mountains white with snow. The water was still and dark, and the silence was broken only by the cry of a bird or the rumble of falling ice. Darwin thought it as wild and beautiful a place as any on the whole voyage.

In the channel Darwin saw great forests of giant kelp, a brown seaweed that grows to many metres in length and clings to the rocks with a rope-like tangle of roots. Among its leaves swarmed fish, shells, crabs and a thousand tiny creatures, and he judged that this underwater forest rivalled any wood of the tropics. If the kelp were ever destroyed, he wrote, vast numbers of animals would perish with it.

Where the glaciers reached the sea, great cliffs of blue ice rose from the water, and the crew watched from their boats in awe. Suddenly an immense mass broke away and plunged into the sea, sending out a huge wave that raced toward the beach where the boats lay. The men ran down the shore and hauled the boats up out of reach just in time, and the wave swept past them, which saved the expedition from disaster.

Darwin watched the Fuegians who lived along these shores, travelling in canoes with their families, and was struck by how hard their life was. They lived on shellfish, seals and berries, slept in simple shelters of branches and moved from place to place as the food ran out. He pitied their poverty, but he also admired their skill in surviving where few Europeans could have lasted a month.

A year after the first visit the Beagle returned to Woollya, and a thin man with long, wild hair came out in a canoe to meet the boat. It was Jemmy Button, wearing nothing but a rag of blanket round his waist, and Darwin wrote that he had never seen so complete and sad a change. The neat young man who had polished his shoes on board was gone, and in his place stood a hungry Fuegian who nevertheless smiled to see his old friends.

That evening Jemmy dined with FitzRoy and ate as neatly as ever with his knife and fork, and he spoke some English with a shy and gentle pride. He had brought presents of otter skins and spearheads, which he had made with his own hands, for the friends who had once taken him to England. He told them that he was happy, that he had a wife, and that he did not want to go back to England.

When the Beagle sailed away, Jemmy lit a great fire on the shore as a farewell signal, and the smoke curled up into the grey sky. Darwin was told that York Minster had robbed Jemmy of his goods and slipped away with Fuegia Basket, and so ended FitzRoy's experiment. Of all the Fuegians he had met, Darwin remembered Jemmy with the greatest fondness.

In the damp beech forests Darwin noticed bunches of round, bright yellow fungi growing on the trunks of the trees, and he learned that the Fuegians eat them. They were almost the only food from the forest that these people had, apart from a few berries, and they were a valuable part of the diet. A fungus that Darwin collected was later named in his honour, and it still carries his name.

Sailing in the Strait of Magellan, Darwin saw Mount Sarmiento, a colossal cone of ice and snow rising straight from the sea to a sharp, shining summit. When the clouds lifted, the sight was so magnificent that it seemed to him one of the grandest of the whole voyage, and the memory stayed vivid for years. It was the very picture of a wild and untouched land, as wide and silent as the sky.

Back in the Falkland Islands, Darwin watched the jackass penguins that stood upright along the shore like little men in dark coats. On land they brayed loudly like donkeys, and they walked with a clumsy waddle, but in the water they dived and swam as swiftly as fish. It seemed to him that such awkward walkers were perfectly made for the sea.

At Santa Cruz the crew ran the Beagle onto a beach at high tide, so that when the water fell she lay on her side and her hull could be scraped and repaired. While the carpenters worked, FitzRoy formed a bold plan: he would take boats up the unexplored river toward the distant Andes. Darwin, who loved any chance to see new country, was keen to go, and the captain was glad to have him.

In April FitzRoy, Darwin and about twenty-five men set off in three whaleboats to explore the Santa Cruz River, with food for three weeks. No one knew where the river began, or how far from the sea they would have to go, and the expedition had the feeling of a voyage into the unknown. Each man was given a share of the heavy load, for there was no room for anything that was not needed.

The current was so strong that rowing was useless, and so the men walked along the bank, hauling the boats upstream with long ropes like horses pulling a barge. Darwin took his turn at the ropes with everyone else, and in the evenings the party cooked guanaco meat over a fire on the stony shore. They slept under the open sky, wrapped in cloaks, with the sound of the river in their ears.

The river flowed through a vast, dry plain between cliffs of black basalt, the hardened lava of ancient volcanoes. Its water was a milky blue and its bed was strewn with stones that had been carried down from the Andes, far away to the west. Darwin noted that few plants broke the dry landscape, and that the plain seemed almost without end.

After about two weeks the travellers caught sight of the snowy Andes, a line of pale peaks glimmering on the horizon. By then half their food was gone, and FitzRoy decided that they must turn back, although the mountains were still far off. It was a disappointment, but all agreed that the captain was right to put the safety of his men first.

The return journey was swift and easy, for the same current that had slowed them now carried the boats downstream almost without help. They covered in a few days the distance that had taken more than two weeks to climb, and they were soon back on board the Beagle. Darwin had seen a new and strange part of the continent, and his boxes were richer by the plants and rocks he had gathered.

The Beagle then sailed into the Strait of Magellan and anchored at Port Famine, a place whose gloomy name comes from the year 1587. In that year the English sailor Thomas Cavendish found there the ruins of a Spanish colony in which nearly all the settlers had died of hunger. The shore was calm and green, but Darwin could not look at it without thinking of those lost lives.

Darwin climbed Mount Tarn, a peak of about eight hundred metres, struggling first through a tangle of beech forest and then over slopes of snow. From the summit he looked out over a wild land of mountains, channels and glaciers, a wilderness in which he could see no sign of human life. Tired and happy, he gathered rock specimens and hurried back to the camp before dark.

In June 1834 the Beagle finally left the narrow channels of the Strait and entered the Pacific Ocean, where huge, slow swells rolled under her keel. After so many months of cold, rain and bare rock, the crew looked forward to the warm sun and the green valleys of Chile. Darwin, as ever, was seasick, but even that could not spoil the pleasure of turning his face to the north.

On 23 July 1834 the Beagle dropped anchor at Valparaíso, in Chile, where white houses climb steep brown hills beneath the tall wall of the Andes. Darwin was delighted to find there an old school friend from Shrewsbury, Richard Corfield, who had become a merchant in the port. His welcome was so warm that Darwin felt as if a piece of home had come to meet him.

After the grey rain and bare rock of the far south, Chile seemed to Darwin a land of sunshine, with brown hills dotted with cactus and a deep blue sky. The air was dry and clear, and the sight of distant mountains with snow on their summits filled him with energy. He felt that a new part of his voyage had begun, and that the Pacific coast would offer him wonders as great as any he had met on the Atlantic side.

In August 1834 Darwin hired a guide named Mariano Gonzales and ten mules, and set out to explore the country for several weeks. The mules followed a mare with a little bell round her neck, called the madrina, and they would not leave her for anything in the world. It was a cheap and simple way of travelling, and it allowed him to wander far from the roads, with all his baggage on the animals' backs.

Darwin rode over dry hills and through fertile green valleys to Santiago, the capital of Chile, and from there he continued south into the country of the mines. Each night he slept wherever the day's ride ended, in a farmhouse, a hut or, if necessary, on the ground beside his saddle. The guide was cheerful and skilled, and the journey passed pleasantly, even when the paths grew steep and the weather turned cold.

In a copper mine Darwin watched the miners climb up steep ladders carrying enormous loads of ore on their backs, and he was astonished at their strength. They made the climb again and again, with no complaint, and they earned very little for it. Darwin felt a deep respect for these men, and he could not help comparing their lot with the ease of those who owned the mine.

Wherever he stopped in the Chilean countryside, Darwin was welcomed with a warmth that moved him. Farmers gave him food and a bed for the night, and often refused to take payment, as if a traveller were an honoured guest rather than a customer. He thought that such generosity was something an Englishman could hardly imagine, and he remembered it fondly for the rest of the journey.

From Santiago the Andes seemed to hang in the air above the city, their snowy summits glowing pink and gold in the evening light. Darwin stared at them for long moments, for he had already begun to dream of crossing the great chain and looking down on the plains of Argentina. The idea grew stronger each day, until it became a plan, and the plan became a promise to himself.

On the hills near the coast Darwin found layers of sea shells embedded in the rock, hundreds of feet above the level of the water. He remembered the white band on St Jago and the gravel terraces of Patagonia, and he realised that the coast of Chile too had been lifted up from the sea. Each new proof made Lyell's teaching seem more certain, and made Darwin more eager for the great test of the mountains.

In late September 1834 Darwin returned to Valparaíso and fell ill with a high fever. It was probably caused by bad food or water, and in a few days he was too weak to leave his bed, with aching limbs and a burning head. There was little anyone could do except let him rest and wait for the fever to run its course.

Richard Corfield nursed Darwin in his own house, and the sick man lay in bed for about a month, growing slowly stronger. He had plenty of time to think about everything he had seen, and he used it to arrange his notes and to write long letters to his family. When at last he was able to walk in the garden, the Chilean sun on his face felt better than any medicine.

On 10 November 1834 the Beagle sailed from Valparaíso for the south, and Darwin, still thin and pale, went on board with his friends. He was grateful to Corfield for his care, and he looked forward to the forests and islands ahead. Though the illness had cost him a month, it had not dimmed his curiosity, and he was soon at his notebooks again.

On the way south the Beagle came to the island of Chiloé, a land of heavy rain, dense forest and small villages scattered along a ragged coast. The dark trees came right down to the water's edge, and the grey sea lay calm beneath a sky that rarely cleared. Though the climate was wet and the days were dim, Darwin found the place strangely beautiful, and he was glad to explore it.

One day on the rocky shore of Chiloé Darwin saw a small, dark fox so absorbed in watching the surveyors at work that it never noticed him approach. He walked quietly right up to it, and the animal was easily taken, which gave him a fine specimen. It proved to be a new species, which is still known as Darwin's fox and lives in the forests of Chile.

The forests of Chiloé were so dense that Darwin could scarcely force a way through them, for the ground was heaped with fallen trunks and covered with bamboo, creepers and giant ferns. Often he had to climb along the horizontal trees instead of walking on the earth, and sometimes he sank to his knees in rotting wood. He emerged from each excursion wet, scratched and delighted, with new plants and insects in his bag.

Darwin rode to Castro, the old capital of the island, a sleepy town of wooden houses where grass grew thickly in the streets and few people were about. The islanders were poor but generous and gentle, and they welcomed the visitors into their homes with unforced courtesy. It was a quiet corner of the world, and Darwin was moved by its simplicity.

The people of Chiloé cooked their meals in a hole in the ground, heating stones in a fire and then piling on shellfish, potatoes and pork under a covering of leaves. Darwin watched the Chilotes prepare this feast, which they called curanto, and he ate it with them and found it simple but delicious. The islanders' way of life seemed hard to him, but there was a cheerful dignity in the way they shared whatever they had.

In the Chonos Islands, south of Chiloé, Darwin found wild potatoes growing among the sand and shells of the beaches, thin plants with small tubers. He knew that they were wild relatives of the potato that fed the people of Europe, and he realised that this wet and rugged coast was part of the true home of the crop. It was a pleasing example of how a humble plant on a remote shore can change the history of the whole world.

On the night of 19 January 1835 Darwin watched the volcano Osorno burst into eruption, a huge red glow spreading across the sky above the black sea. Showers of glowing fragments shot up from the crater and fell again, and the mountain seemed to burn like a great beacon. Even from many miles away the sight was so grand that he could scarcely turn his eyes from it.

Darwin later learned that two other volcanoes had erupted at almost the same moment, one in the high Andes and one far away in Central America. The coincidence set him wondering whether such mountains are linked by some hidden source of fire deep beneath the surface of the earth. It was a bold thought for its time, and he turned it over for many years afterward.

In February 1835 the Beagle reached Valdivia, a small town of low houses nestled in a forest of Chile, famed throughout the region for its apples. The country was green and peaceful, with orchards, clearings and a calm river winding through the woods. Darwin was looking forward to a quiet week of exploring, and had no idea of what lay ahead.

Darwin strolled through the orchards of Valdivia, where the branches were bent under the weight of ripe apples and the ground was littered with fruit. The people made cider from the harvest, and children carried baskets of apples as freely as other children carry sweets. It was a scene of peace and plenty, and Darwin could not know that the next day the ground itself would turn against him.

On 20 February 1835 Darwin was resting on the ground in a forest near Valdivia, enjoying the quiet of a warm late morning, when the earth gave a sudden shudder. A powerful earthquake rolled through the woods, and the tall trees began to sway as if a great wind had caught them. For a moment Darwin lay still, unable to understand what was happening to the ground beneath him.

The earthquake lasted about two minutes, and it seemed far longer to Darwin, who found that he could hardly keep his balance. He said that the sensation was like walking on thin ice that bends and trembles beneath the feet of the walker. All around him the forest creaked and groaned, and the ground rippled as if it were made of water.

Darwin wrote that a bad earthquake destroys our oldest ideas in a single moment. The earth, which we have always thought of as the very symbol of solidity, had moved under his feet like the thin crust of something fluid, and nothing seemed safe any more. In the short space of a minute or two, he felt a sense of insecurity that no amount of thinking could have given him.

At Valdivia the damage was slight, and the townspeople were more frightened than hurt, but the sea behaved strangely and everyone sensed that something greater had happened elsewhere. Boats rocked in the harbour, and the tide seemed to behave in a way that no one could explain. Soon news came that the city of Concepción, many miles to the north, had suffered terribly.

On 4 March 1835 the Beagle reached Concepción and the nearby port of Talcahuano, and what the crew saw was astonishing. Both towns lay in ruins, with the walls tumbled and the roofs broken, and the shore was strewn with timber and furniture as if a thousand ships had been wrecked. Darwin, who had seen many wonders, wrote that it was bitter to see in one minute the work of years destroyed.

Most of the people had escaped with their lives, because the shock had been slow enough to let them run out of their houses into the open air. They now camped in rough huts made of branches, and the children played among the ruins as if nothing had happened. Darwin reflected that if the earthquake had come at night, many more would have died.

After the shaking stopped, a great wave had rolled in from the sea and swept over the shore, carrying boats, timber and furniture far inland. Darwin was told that the water had first drawn back from the coast, so that the bottom of the bay lay bare, and then returned with terrible force. The ruined houses and tumbled boats were silent witnesses of the power that had been unleashed.

Darwin and FitzRoy measured the shore around Concepción and found that the land had risen by two or three feet. Beds of mussels that had once lived under the sea were now dead and dry, and they lay stranded far above the tide with a terrible smell. Here, before their eyes, was proof that the ground could be lifted in a single morning, just as Lyell had said it could.

At Santa Maria island the land had risen even more, by about three metres at the southern end, and Darwin walked over old mussel beds and rotting shells that now lay high above the reach of the waves. He looked at rocks that had lately been covered by the sea, and now stood well out of the water. These changes were exactly what Darwin needed to understand how the Andes themselves might have been built.

Darwin concluded that earthquakes and volcanoes come from the same cause, deep inside the earth, and that the forces which shake the land also lift it, little by little. If a single shock could raise the coast by a few feet, then a long series of shocks over thousands of years could raise a whole range of mountains. The idea gave him a way of understanding the Andes, and he longed to climb them to see the evidence for himself.

In March 1835 Darwin returned to Santiago and set out again with Mariano Gonzales and a train of mules, this time with a daring aim. He meant to cross the Andes, the immense mountain chain which divides Chile from Argentina, and to see with his own eyes the rocks of which he had dreamed. The guide knew the passes well, and the mules, led by their bell-wearing mare, were strong and sure-footed.

The party followed a deep valley whose steep walls rose sharply on both sides while a loud river foamed and thundered far below. The path was narrow and sometimes ran along the edge of a precipice, so that the mules stepped carefully and Darwin trusted his animal completely. Each day they climbed higher, and the vegetation grew thinner until only rock and snow remained.

Near the top the snow lay deep, and the line of mules and men slowly crossed the high pass of Portillo in the thin, bitterly cold air. The peaks around them were white against a dark blue sky, and every sound seemed to carry for miles. Darwin, wrapped in his heaviest clothes, felt both very small and very fortunate to be there.

In a cliff near the highest pass Darwin found fossil seashells embedded in the rock, more than 3,500 metres above the level of the sea. He stood speechless for a moment, for here, among snow and condors, lay the remains of creatures that had once lived on the bottom of the ocean. It was the clearest possible proof that the whole range had been lifted up from beneath the waves.

From the highest pass Darwin looked eastward over a vast plain that spread out as flat and wide as the sea, and the contrast with the tumbled mountains of Chile took his breath away. He noticed too that the plants and insects on the two sides of the chain were quite different, as if the mountains were the wall of a gigantic fortress dividing two separate worlds. The observation would one day bear fruit in his thinking about how living things spread across the earth.

In the thin air Darwin found that he could not climb without gasping for breath, and his mules stopped often to rest. His guide blamed the snow, but Darwin was sure that the real cause was the great height of the pass. This was his first experience of mountain sickness, and he admitted that it was far from pleasant.

East of the mountains Darwin reached Mendoza, a pleasant town of vineyards, fig trees and peaches lying on a dry plain beneath the shadow of the Andes. The fruit was delicious after the hard climb, and the people greeted the traveller with an easy courtesy. He rested for several days, writing up his notes and drying the specimens that he had collected on the way.

At the village of Luxan a blood-sucking insect called the benchuca came into the hut where Darwin was sleeping and bit him, as he later recorded. Some modern scientists believe that such a bite may have given him a lasting illness, though the matter is still debated and nobody can be sure. Whatever the truth, he suffered poor health for much of his later life, and the benchuca has become part of the Darwin story.

On the return journey, by way of the Uspallata pass, Darwin came upon a group of fossil trees standing upright on a bare mountain slope. They had grown on dry land, then sunk beneath the sea and been buried under thick layers of lava and mud, and finally lifted again to a great height. Reading this tale in the stones, he felt like a man who had learned a language that the earth itself was speaking.

Looking out from the heights of the Andes, Darwin concluded that this vast chain had been raised bit by bit over a very long time, through earthquakes and the pressure of molten rock. Lyell had taught that small changes, repeated for ages, could add up to great ones, and now Darwin had seen the proof with his own eyes. As he sat on a rock with his notebook in the evening light, he understood that the world was far older and more restless than most people believed.

Darwin rejoined the Beagle, which sailed north along a brown and barren coast where almost nothing grew. For hundreds of miles there was hardly a tree, and the mountains rose bare and rust-coloured from the edge of the sea. He looked at the emptiness with a geologist's eye, and noted how clearly the rocks displayed their history in a land without plants to hide them.

In June 1835 Darwin rode to Copiapó through desert valleys where rain falls only rarely, and where a green farm can exist only beside a thin stream. A few miles from the river the land was completely dry, and there was hardly a leaf, a blade of grass or an insect to be seen. He found it strange to cross such a barren waste on a mule, with only the sound of hooves for company.

At Iquique there was no fresh water at all, and it had to be brought in by boat from a town many miles away. Darwin visited the nitre works on the plain behind the town, where workers dug up a white salty earth and refined it into saltpetre, which was used to make fertiliser. The place seemed miserable and lifeless, and yet it was the source of a valuable trade that crossed the sea to Europe.

In July 1835 the Beagle reached Callao, the port of Lima, in Peru, and Darwin travelled inland to see the capital. A grey mist hung over the whole district, and rain almost never fell, so that the land around was dusty and dull beneath a heavy sky. Darwin, who had been spoiled by the green forests of Brazil and Chiloé, found it a most unattractive place.

In Lima Darwin was fascinated by the women, who wore tight black veils that covered everything except one bright eye. He found the city itself dirty and decaying, though it had once been one of the richest and grandest in South America. The great churches and old houses seemed to him monuments to a world that was fading.

Near Callao Darwin saw the ruins of the old port, which had been destroyed in 1746 by an earthquake and a gigantic sea wave. The wave had thrown ships far inland, and the broken walls still stood in the sand, with the sea gently lapping at the shore as if nothing had happened. It was a lesson in the destructive power of the ground and the water, and Darwin remembered Concepción.

On the island of San Lorenzo, off Callao, Darwin found layers of sea shells about twenty-five metres above the water, and among them he discovered pieces of string and corn. These humble things were made by people, and so they proved that the coast had risen since men first lived there. It was a wonderful discovery, for it showed that the changes of the land continued even within human history.

FitzRoy had more than twenty chronometers on board, and he checked them again and again against the stars, for his purpose was to measure the distances round the whole world with unusual exactness. The task needed patience, a steady hand and a quiet mind, and Darwin admired the captain's devotion to it. Each careful reading was a small stone laid in the great structure of the voyage.

On 7 September 1835 the Beagle left Peru and sailed west across the open Pacific toward the Galápagos Islands, a place of which Darwin knew very little. The trade wind filled the sails, and the ship ran steadily over a blue sea, with flying fish leaping from the crests. He stood at the rail in the evening and wondered what the strange islands would show him.

On 15 September 1835 the crew sighted the Galápagos Islands, a group of black volcanic islands that lie across the equator. They saw low hills, bare slopes and small cones like the heaps beside an ironworks, and no one on board knew what strange creatures lived there. The Beagle would spend five weeks among the islands, and for Darwin it would prove one of the most important stays of the whole voyage.

On Chatham Island, the first of the Galápagos that Darwin visited, the ground was black volcanic rock, hot underfoot and covered with scrubby bushes that seemed to have no leaves at all. The sun beat down, the surf crashed on the black lava, and the whole scene was so strange and silent that it seemed to belong to another world. Darwin pushed on regardless, with his hammer in his hand and his bags empty, ready to be filled.

On the black rocks of the shore Darwin watched the marine iguanas, large dark lizards that swim in the cold sea and feed on seaweed. He thought them hideous creatures, and called them imps of darkness, but he was fascinated all the same. When he threw one far out into the water it swam straight back to the spot where he stood, as if the shore were the only refuge it knew.

On James Island Darwin camped for several days with a few of his men, and he found the place swarming with land iguanas, yellow-brown lizards that dug burrows in the soft ground. There were so many burrows that it was hard to find a place for the tent, and every step had to be taken with care. The creatures ate cactus and then lay in the sun, and they seemed quite unconcerned about the strangers.

Giant tortoises plodded along well-worn paths from the lowlands to the springs in the hills, and Darwin watched them with great interest. He timed one, and found that it covered only about four miles a day, including stops to eat. He learned that the first sailors to visit the islands had found water by following the paths of the tortoises, which led straight to the springs.

Darwin rode on the back of a giant tortoise, a seat that was not easy to balance on, and he was amused by its slow and solemn walk. The vice-governor of the islands, Nicholas Lawson, told him that he could tell from the shell which island a tortoise had come from. Darwin only half listened at the time, and did not guess how important the remark would later prove.

The sailors of the Beagle took live tortoises on board for food, because the great animals can live for months without eating and so provide fresh meat on a long voyage. Whalers and pirates had done the same for many years, and so many had been taken that on some of the islands the tortoises were becoming scarce. Darwin could see that the hunting was a threat to them, though he could hardly have imagined how serious it would become.

Darwin noticed that the mockingbirds from different islands seemed slightly different from each other, and he took care to note which islands they came from. In his notes he wrote that if this was really so, the animals of such island groups would be well worth studying, for the facts might shake the old belief that species never change. At that moment he was only beginning to understand what he had found, and the full meaning was still hidden from him.

On the islands Darwin collected many small finches, dull brown and black birds that did not look at all remarkable. Sadly he did not write down which island each one had come from, and only later did he learn that they belonged to many distinct kinds, each with a beak of a different shape. Fortunately FitzRoy and others had labelled their own collections, and from these Darwin was later able to repair his mistake.

The animals of the Galápagos had never learned to fear people, and they were wonderfully tame. Darwin once pushed a hawk off a branch with the end of his gun, and a mockingbird alighted on a pitcher he was holding and drank from it as calmly as if he were part of the scenery. He remarked that fear of man is something an animal must learn, and that it takes many generations to become fixed.

As he sailed away, Darwin saw that nearly every island had its own kinds of animals, all of them related to those of South America, which lies about a thousand kilometres to the east. He later wrote that the archipelago was a little world within itself, and the thought began to trouble him: how had such a world come to be filled with life, and why was each part of it a little different? The answer would take him many years of patient work, and a great deal of courage, to find.

In late October 1835 the Beagle left the Galápagos and began a long voyage across the open Pacific, with the trade wind steady behind her. For more than three weeks there was no land at all, only a wide blue sea, flying fish that skimmed the waves and an empty sky. Darwin spent the long days arranging his notes and trying to make sense of the strange islands he had left behind.

In the Low Archipelago Darwin saw for the first time a true coral island, a thin ring of white sand and palm trees enclosing a lagoon of smooth green water. On the outer side the surf thundered against the reef, but inside all was calm, and the contrast fascinated him. He stood at the rail and stared at it for a long while, for he had read of such places, and now he saw one.

On 15 November 1835 the Beagle dropped anchor off Tahiti, an island of high green mountains and white beaches fringed with palms. The air was warm and sweet with the scent of flowers, and canoes crowded round the ship while the islanders laughed and shouted greetings. Darwin, ever eager, was impatient to leave the ship and see the valleys that rose behind the shore.

The Tahitians welcomed the visitors with fruit, laughter and flowers woven into their hair, and Darwin found them gentle, handsome and good-humoured. Their faces were open and kind, and they treated strangers with a courtesy which many a European might have envied. The first sight of them gave him a high opinion of their character, and it never changed.

Darwin set out into the interior with two guides, who carried food and water in tubes of bamboo and moved through the forest with an easy, tireless stride. On the way they caught small fish in the stream with their bare hands, wrapped them in leaves and baked them over hot stones. Darwin ate the meal with relish, and thought it the best he had had for a long time.

The party climbed a steep cliff with the help of ropes, and from the top they looked down on a wide valley full of waterfalls, tree ferns and fruit trees. That night they slept under a shelter made of leaves, and Darwin noticed that his guides knelt and said a prayer before they lay down to rest. In the soft light and the sound of falling water, the moment seemed to him full of peace.

On Sunday Darwin attended a service in a Tahitian church, where the congregation sat in neat clothes and listened to the sermon with quiet attention. Although he could not follow the words, he was struck by the orderly manner of the people and by the gentle sound of their singing. It was a very different picture from the wild and savage island that some travellers had described.

Before the voyage Darwin had heard people say that the missionaries had spoiled Tahiti, but his own visit changed his mind. He saw that the islanders had become more peaceful and more honest, and he wrote that anyone who spoke lightly of the missions ought to see the island for himself. At the same time he admitted that the old ways were fading, and that this was not all gain.

From a high place on the mountain Darwin saw the neighbouring island of Eimeo, ringed by a white line of surf where the waves broke on a barrier reef. Inside the reef the water lay calm and pale, and the island rose from it like a jewel in a setting. The sight matched the idea that was forming in his mind about how coral reefs and rings are built, and he made careful sketches.

On 26 November 1835 the Beagle weighed anchor and left Tahiti, bound for New Zealand, and the green island sank slowly into the haze behind her. Darwin was seasick again, and he was sorry to be leaving the friendly valleys where he had been so happy. Yet he carried away a store of fresh ideas and good memories, and the thought of the next landfall drew him on.

In December 1835 the Beagle reached the Bay of Islands in New Zealand, where Darwin found an English mission planted among the villages of the Maori. The neat houses, the white-painted church and the trim gardens seemed so out of place in that wild land that he could hardly believe his eyes. Beyond the cleared fields, the hills were covered with dark bush, and from them came the calls of unfamiliar birds.

Darwin met the Maori, a proud and energetic people whose faces were tattooed with elaborate curving lines, and he admired their fine build and their quick intelligence. They seemed to him very different from the Fuegians, and far more able to deal with Europeans on equal terms. He noted too that the men often wore a cloak of woven flax over their shoulders, and carried a spear or a musket at their sides.

Darwin walked inland to Waimate, a mission farm where wheat, barley and English flowers grew behind neat hedges in the middle of the New Zealand bush. The missionaries had made the farm with the help of Maori workers, and the sight of a quiet English village in such a place filled Darwin with astonishment. He slept in a comfortable house, and for a few hours he could almost forget that he was on the far side of the world.

At Kororareka, a rough little port on the bay, Darwin saw sailors and settlers drinking and fighting in the muddy streets. He was shocked that so many Englishmen should behave so badly so far from home, and he judged the place to be a very bad example to the Maori. It made him think that civilisation does not always follow the flag, and that the good influence of the missions was struggling against a harsher tide.

On 30 December 1835 the Beagle left New Zealand, and Darwin wrote that everyone on board was glad to go. He found the country less pleasant than Tahiti, with its cold rains and its quarrelsome settlers, and he looked forward to the warm sun of Australia. The bay faded behind the stern, and ahead lay a voyage of about two weeks over the Tasman Sea.

In January 1836 the Beagle reached Sydney, a bright new town of stone houses and busy streets beside a beautiful harbour. Darwin was astonished that so fine a city could have grown in less than fifty years from a small settlement of convicts and soldiers. He walked through the streets with growing admiration for the energy of his countrymen, though he could not help noticing the heavy price that others had paid.

Darwin rode inland across the Blue Mountains with a guide, through woods of gum trees whose pale bark hung in loose strips. He noticed that the leaves hang edgeways, so that they give very little shade, and that the forest looks much the same for mile after mile. It was a landscape quite unlike any he had seen, and the endless grey-green sameness seemed to him a little sad.

In the bush beyond the mountains Darwin watched a platypus swimming in a quiet pond, and then an ant-lion trapping ants in a pit of sand. The platypus was unlike any other animal, and yet the ant-lion's pit was just like those of Europe, so that he found himself wondering whether two different Creators had been at work. He decided that one hand, and one plan, lay behind it all, though the puzzle of why Australia was so different from the rest of the world remained.

One night near Bathurst Darwin watched a gathering of Aboriginal people dance by firelight, their bodies painted with white lines, in a corroboree that lasted for hours. He admired their skill as trackers and hunters, and he wrote sadly that wherever Europeans had settled, death seemed to pursue the Aboriginal people. The glow of the fire on their moving figures stayed in his memory long after he had left the clearing.

In February 1836 the Beagle reached Hobart, in Van Diemen's Land, a pretty town of white houses below a tall mountain with a cap of cloud. Darwin learned that the island's Aboriginal people had all been taken away by the settlers and moved to a small island in Bass Strait, and he regretted it deeply. He was impatient now to turn homeward, though more than half the world still lay between him and England.

In April 1836 the Beagle reached the Keeling Islands, a ring of coral and palm trees surrounding a quiet lagoon in the Indian Ocean. The land lay only a few metres above the waves, and a visitor standing on the beach seemed to be at the very edge of the sea. Darwin, who had longed to examine such a place, hurried ashore with his notebooks and a heart full of questions.

On the outer edge of the reef the surf thundered all day against a living wall of coral, and yet it could not break it down. Darwin saw that a pink seaweed and a hardy kind of coral held the barrier firm against the weight of the ocean. He wrote with admiration of these soft and tiny creatures, which could build a rampart strong enough to defy the greatest waves.

On the islands Darwin learned about the robber crab, a huge land crab that lives in burrows under the palm trees and feeds on coconuts. The inhabitants told him that it climbs the trunks and tears the husks from the nuts, and then hammers at them with its powerful claws until they break. Darwin thought it one of the most curious and surprising animals that he had met on the whole voyage.

Darwin now saw, with a clearness that thrilled him, how a ring of coral islands comes into being. A volcanic island slowly sinks beneath the sea, while the coral growing round its edge builds steadily upward, until the island has vanished and only a ring of reef is left around a quiet lagoon. It was a simple and beautiful idea, and it explained a mystery that had puzzled sailors for generations.

At Mauritius, an island in the Indian Ocean, a hospitable English officer took Darwin into his home and treated him as an old friend. Darwin rode through fields of sugar cane and gazed at the jagged mountains, whose strange shapes rose steeply from the plain. After the long weeks at sea, the green island with its warm breezes and kindly people seemed a pleasant dream.

At Cape Town, in South Africa, Darwin and FitzRoy went to visit the famous astronomer Sir John Herschel at his house among the gardens below Table Mountain. Darwin felt deeply honoured to meet one of the greatest scientists of the age, whose books had inspired him long before he left England. Years later he would quote Herschel's famous phrase about the origin of new species, which Herschel called the mystery of mysteries.

At St Helena Darwin walked up a quiet valley to the grave of Napoleon, which lay beneath a willow tree beside a spring. He saw too that goats had eaten the island's original forest, and that most of the plants now growing there had been brought from other lands. It was a vivid lesson in how quickly human beings and their animals can change the living face of a place.

At Ascension Darwin found a bundle of letters from home, and they filled him with joy. His sisters wrote that Henslow had read his notes to a meeting of scientists at Cambridge, and that the great geologist Sedgwick had said that Darwin would take a place among the leading naturalists of Europe. He walked about in a happy daze, for he had hardly dared to hope that his work was known at all.

To check his chronometers once more, FitzRoy turned back toward Bahia, in the wrong direction for England, and Darwin was furious at the delay. He wrote that he hated the sea and all the ships that sail upon it, and when at last he saw Brazil again he was glad to think that he would never visit a land of slaves again. The mild air and fine colours of the coast could not cheer him, for his mind was fixed on home.

From Bahia the Beagle sailed on to the Azores, a group of green islands in the Atlantic, and then turned north toward England. Autumn storms rocked the ship and soaked the decks, but Darwin could think only of the smell of English fields. Each day he marked the distance that still lay between him and the shores he had left almost five years before.

On 2 October 1836 the Beagle came into Falmouth, on the south-west coast of England, after four years and nine months away. The sailors cheered, but Darwin, who had been so often seasick, felt a quiet joy that was almost too deep for words. He hurried ashore at once, eager to find a coach that would take him home.

Darwin travelled north by coach for two days, rattling through the quiet autumn lanes of England, and he reached Shrewsbury late at night on 4 October. The great house stood dark and silent, and he was soon asleep in his old room. He did not know it, but he was already a man of whom the scientists of London had begun to speak.

At breakfast next morning Darwin walked into the room to the great surprise of his sisters and his father. Dr Darwin looked at him closely for a long moment, and then remarked to the girls that the shape of his head was quite altered. It was the doctor's way of saying that his son had left a boy and come home a man, and everyone laughed and wept at once.

Darwin soon began to share his collections with the experts of London and Cambridge. Richard Owen examined the fossil bones from South America, and John Gould studied the birds, while other scholars took the insects, the fish and the plants. It would take years to describe all that he had gathered, and Darwin worked among them with tireless interest.

In 1837 Gould told Darwin that the small birds from the Galápagos, which Darwin had thought were a mixture of different families, were really a group of closely related finches, each of a separate kind. He said that the mockingbirds of the different islands were distinct as well, and Darwin, who had carelessly mixed his labels, had to ask FitzRoy and others to share their notes. It was a bitter lesson in the need for exactness, but it showed him the full meaning of what he had seen.

In 1837 Darwin began a series of secret notebooks about the way species change, filling them with questions, guesses and small sketches. On one page he drew a little tree with branches, and above it he wrote the words I think, to show how new kinds might grow from old ones like twigs from a single trunk. It was the first picture of an idea that would one day shake the world.

In 1838 Darwin read a famous essay on population by Thomas Malthus, and suddenly he saw how the struggle for life might change living things. Those animals and plants that were best fitted to their surroundings would survive and leave offspring, and over very long periods the result would be new species. He worked on the idea for twenty years, in quiet and in ill health, and in 1859 he published it in his book On the Origin of Species.

In 1839 Darwin published the story of his journey, and it soon became a favourite with the public, who loved its clear pictures of strange lands. It went through many printings, and later readers have called it The Voyage of the Beagle. Even today it is read for its sharp eyes, its honest wonder and its flashes of humour.

The Beagle herself made one more long survey voyage, to Australia, and then she became a watch ship on the coast of England, where she lay quietly in a river mouth. In 1870 she was sold and broken up, and her timbers were sold for scrap. Yet her name is now known all over the world, because of the young man who sailed in her in 1831.

Looking back in old age, Darwin judged the voyage of the Beagle to have been by far the most important event of his life, since it set the whole course of his career. The ship had taught him to look, to collect, to question and to think in terms of vast spans of time, and from those habits came his later books. FitzRoy, too, found a new calling, for as head of an early weather office he is credited with the word forecast and with warnings that saved many sailors.
